Another book Individual Psychotherapy and the Science of Psychodynamics (1979) became a favourite textbook on psychotherapy trainings in the 1980s. Shiri Spector  

This paper is an attempt to present and discuss the application of psychodynamic thinking and practice to working with people with epilepsy. The paper provides a general explanation of what epilepsy is, followed by a brief review of the existing psychoanalytic literature in relation to epilepsy. The core of the paper is a detailed case study describing a time-limited psychodynamic counselling with a patient in an epilepsy outpatient clinic at a large general hospital in the UK. This account aims to highlight some of the issues and themes in working with people with epilepsy, and to add to the limited literature available on psychodynamic work with this client group.

Amélie Noack and Lisa Baraitser

Lisa Baraitser

1 Daleham Gardens, London NW3 5BY. [email: AmelieNoac@aol.com]

[l.baraitser@psychology.bbk.ac.uk]

Lisa Baraitser  

This paper presents some thoughts about working clinically with mothers who have been sexually abused in childhood. We review the research literature that indicates that survivor mothers face interpersonal difficulties relating to their children, and, in the light of this research, suggest that survivor mothers may benefit from a therapeutic service that is specifically designed to meet their needs. We draw on recent explorations of transgenerational processes in the transmission of trauma to present an understanding of the psychodynamics involved in the difficulties survivors have with mothering. This understanding informs the design and implementation of groups for survivor mothers at the Maya Centre, a psychodynamic counselling centre for women living in poverty in the London Borough of Islington. Clinical examples taken from three short-term therapeutic groups are presented and discussed.

Closeness and Intimacy

Nigel Burch

Nigel Burch

29a Northampton Square, London EC1V 0ES. [email: nigelburch@tiscali.co.uk]

Nigel Burch  

In this paper I am trying to open up a line of thinking that has been developing in my mind for some years. I start by defining what I mean by closeness and intimacy. Then I describe what led me into thinking about the topic of closeness and intimacy, a topic not often touched on in analytic training or writing. I then describe something that happened in a session that struck me as unusual. I go on to look at three papers that came to my mind in this context, and then discuss the development of my thoughts. I conclude that closeness and intimacy - which I see as having a more powerful effect on a patient than closeness - are mutative phenomena in their own right, as well as being an essential part of therapy.

Marguerite Valentine

Marguerite Valentine

39 Womersley Road, London N8 9AP. [email: marguerite@f2s.com]

Marguerite Valentine  

Working with severely disturbed patients is one of the most challenging and difficult areas for the psychotherapist in private practice. Not only is there an ever present risk of a psychotic episode but, worse, the patient may threaten or actually commit suicide. The following gives an account of one such patient. Describing the typical ambience of the sessions, it tracks the developing realization for the therapist of the patient's involvement with the psychiatric system, and the consequent ethical dilemmas, which remained unresolved. Finally, it considers from the therapist's point of view what factors may have led to the patient's suicide.

Nicola Glucksmann

Nicola Glucksmann

London

Nicola Glucksmann  

It would be disingenuous - and an attack on the spirit of this book - were I not to reveal my own hand before considering it for review. Eight years ago, I had a single child followed by twins 15 months later. All three children were the result of ART (assisted reproductive technology). They were fertilized embryos, all from the same IVF cycle but defrosted at different times, and born after four years of failed treatments. Like so many women described in this book, I had everything from invasive surgery, injections in my stomach, hormone treatments, keyhole surgery, four cycles of artificial inseminations and a failed IVF attempt. It was, in hindsight, a multiple trauma which robbed me of my capacity to think. This is a book about thinking, in the broadest sense, and about how difficult it is to hold on to that capacity when in the grip of very powerful emotions.

All infertility treatment takes place in a climate of trauma, elation and persecutory loss. All couples walk into clinics not only with a history of bereavement, because the baby has not yet materialized, but also often with a manic optimism in the belief that if they are ‘positive’ then ‘it’ will work. And implicit in their hope that ‘it’ will ‘work’ is the persecutory idea that they themselves don't. When the intervention fails too, that shame can infect doctor and patients alike undermining their capacity to think - to consider whether perhaps it might be time to stop - and threatening the chance for healing and recovery.

Drawing on their own personal emotional investment in the world of infertility, the 16 different contributors to this book offer a highly creative, intelligent and innovative approach to a psychological crisis. The book is divided into four sections: the experience of infertility, the psychological aspects, changing patterns of kinship and the shadow. Each section considers the same issues but from the very different perspectives of the writers involved. It will, I hope, prove to be a template for many other books in the future. The one unifying belief among all those contributing is that a technological whirlwind of hope and new possibilities has been created by ART - a whirlwind in which mind and body have often spun apart. All seem to agree that we need to restore a link between the two and try to counter the potential for this splitting.

Introduction

Over a career spanning nearly 50 years, Edna O'Shaughnessy has been actively involved in the fields of child and adult analysis, working in a busy private practice and involved with the Association of Child Psychotherapists, the British Institute of Psychoanalysis and the London Kleinians. She has supervised, analysed and taught numerous psychotherapists and psychoanalysts, employing her dedication, keen insight, and lively imagination not only in the consulting room, but on many committees, conference podiums, editorial meetings and a variety of teaching venues. Drawn by her arresting ideas and fluent writing capacities, I approached her first to request case consultations and then with the hope of persuading her to publish more of her material. We reached a compromise by agreeing on a taped conversation for this Journal. A list of her articles appears at the end of this conversation.

Jean Arundale

Surrealism: Desire Unbound (Tate Modern, London, 20 September 2001-1 January 2002)

John Birtchnell

John Birtchnell

London

John Birtchnell  

The surrealist movement originated in Paris in the 1920s and, during the interwar years, it spread to many countries in Europe and beyond. It began as a literary movement but assumed its fullest expression as an art movement. In her excellent guide to the exhibition, Jennifer Mundy (2001) wrote:

For the surrealists, desire was a weapon against the forces in society, and within the psyche, which would censor the human spirit and repress individual liberty; and love, poetry and the free expression of desire were the ultimate goals. (p. 9)

Conroy Maddox considered there to be a political component to surrealism. He argued that it both dissociated itself from the values of capitalist culture and struggled against it (Levy 1997). Mundy considered the surrealists to be united in a fierce and uncompromising rejection of the economic, legal and religious structures in society that allowed love to all but drown in a sea of convention and hypocrisy. They seemed to consider themselves to be a kind of brotherhood, with a revolutionary zeal. In the exhibition there were a number of group photographs, some including as many as 25 members. The surrealist movement was led by the charismatic André Breton, who was predominantly a poet. A preoccupation of the surrealist poets was a celebration of the union of lovers, both spiritually and carnally. In 1930, with Paul Eluard, Breton wrote, ‘The arms and thighs of the man are bound to the arms and thighs of the woman, wind mixes with smoke, hands take the imprint of desires’ (displayed on a wall of the exhibition). Not very inspiring, but you get the idea. Breton remained a uniting force within the movement until his death in 1966. His art output was not great, neither in quantity nor quality, but he has remained one of the most frequently cited of the surrealists, largely because of what he wrote. He considered the main thrust of surrealism to be a turning away from the external object and a focusing upon what he called internal perception. This process was given the name visuality. There was a conviction among the surrealists as, of course, there is among many psychoanalysts, that the so-called interior world is more important than the exterior world, and the endeavour of the surrealists was to make contact with it and give expression to it.

Introduction

Nathan Field  

It is most gratifying to see this little ‘post-Platonic dialogue’ reprinted in the 20th anniversary issue of the BJP. ‘The Symposium’ was an attempt to express an analytic idea in a more vivid idiom than the familiar clinical/theoretical paper. Given the current restrictions on the presentation of confidential clinical material, it may become increasingly necessary to find new ways of disseminating psychotherapeutic ideas in the future.

When ‘The Symposium’ first appeared many readers assumed Dr W could only be Donald Winnicott. At the time I thought I had simply invented a composite of my ideal psychotherapist. With hindsight I realize now how much the ideas of Donald Winnicott had permeated my thinking.

At a more conscious level I had in mind a different Dr W: the late, much loved Dr Heinz Woolf. He certainly fitted my image of the ideal psychotherapist. But by the time I met him he had retired. Much later I had the good fortune to find another gifted psychotherapist, one to whom I have reason to be profoundly grateful. But, at the end of the day, I suppose the Dr W of this paper describes the kind of therapist all of us would wish, but inevitably fail, to become.

The Symposium: A Post-Platonic Dialogue on the Experience of Psychotherapy

First Published in Bjp 7(2), 1990

Sexuality and Discourses of Psychotherapy

Dick Blackwell

Dick Blackwell

London NW3 5BY

Dick Blackwell  

Dear Editor

It is regrettable in this day and age that it should be necessary to defend the right of ‘free speech’ in an analytic psychotherapy journal. It is perhaps a comment on the general state of the whole discourse and perhaps of its current petit bourgeois tendencies, or perhaps it's just certain factions within the discourse.

BJP 20:1 contained letters from James Taylor (pp. 85-90) and A.J. McGuire (pp. 90-92) suggesting that an article with which they disagreed and of which they disapproved should not have been published by the Journal. BJP 20:2 contained replies from the author of the offending article (Harold Bourne) and from the editor at the time (Jean Arundale). The debate about the content of the article itself is interesting and very much the sort of thing we need in the analytic psychotherapy discourse. What is regrettable is the call for censorship of unpopular, controversial or even outdated views, and that neither Harold Bourne nor Jean Arundale challenge the proposal for censorship on the grounds of the right to free speech. Indeed Jean Arundale goes so far as to express sorrow for offence having been caused. But offence is precisely what has provoked the debate which censorship would have denied us.

James Taylor in his letter actually went further in announcing his support for the editorial view expressed in BJP 19:3 (pp. 399) that the term ‘rabid Kleinians’, used in a book review, was ‘inappropriate and inflammatory language not seemly for a learned journal’. Yet more censorship. And a reference to the fact that Jean Arundale had already agreed that the journal should have censored this particular phrase.

Personally, I find the offending phrase vivid and evocative, and as such entirely appropriate for the discourse of psychotherapy, which is presumably supposed to address, among other things, the outer reaches of human consciousness and behaviour, not to mention human unconsciousness. As Theodor Adorno memorably put it, ‘In psychoanalysis nothing is true except the exaggerations’. Of all people, the Kleinians, particularly those who might merit the offending epithet, are surely able to stand up for themselves and fight their own corner without needing the protection of the official censor.

Sexuality and Discourses of Psychotherapy

James Taylor

James Taylor

Leeds
[email: james.taylor@ntlworld.com]

James Taylor  

Dear Editor

The tenor of Harold Bourne's response (BJP 20(2): 255) to my criticisms (BJP 20(1): 85-90) of his paper, ‘A homosexual turns to women’ (BJP 19(3): 349-54) was unsurprising. His reply is almost entirely ad hominem and fails to respond to any of my or Alec McGuire's substantive points. He implies his age and life experience privilege his position in debate and suggests that I/we wrote in defence of the ‘purity’, ‘innocence’ and ‘health’ of our (sic) sexuality, that I/we lack a sense of humour and I/we were motivated by ‘political correctness’ to ‘muzzle, censor and silence’ him. He also claims that I/we lack the capacity to ‘… stop and think and look deeper … let alone get worried and clinical’. Yet it is precisely the latter capacities that motivated our responses as his paper. We were both suggesting what he had to say, amongst other things, ran contrary to our clinical experience.

My concern was not for political correctness; however I am interested in social justice and accordingly endeavour to extend to clients a commensurate respect and open-mindedness. Learning from this experience inevitably means departures from available but unconvincing metapsychology. I am not, as Bourne suggests, part of a ‘Freud-battering industry’, rather someone who like Freud is interested in revising provisional understandings to reach better understandings. Juliet Mitchell observed that we need to ‘… reflect on the absence of the castration complex, not in our theories but in the cases that confront us’ (Mitchell 1998). So I am interested in asking ‘What kinds of new understandings could be reached if the old ones about so-called “castration anxiety” were eschewed?’ Do we see it because it is there or because it is the vocabulary we have formerly used to describe certain experiences?

407

Change for the Better: Self-help Through Practical Psychotherapy by Elizabeth Wilde McCormick. Published by Continuum Books, London, 2002; 258 pages.

Chess Denman

Chess Denman

Cambridge

Chess Denman  

Change for the Better was the original, self-help Cognitive Analytic Therapy book. It has proved a durable text that has withstood the test of time and also vagaries of various changes of publisher (the first and second editions were published by Cassell in 1990 and 1996). It provides patients and quite a few therapists with an introduction to the basic principles of CAT in a readable and logically presented format. Unlike many self-help books, it manages the difficult task of making some quite complicated ideas easily accessible without becoming patronizing or unduly trite.

The book starts with a section on ‘Change’, which tries to guide the reader towards an understanding of the main ways in which life can go wrong and the sort of things that they might expect to change as a result of working through the book. It then moves into a more meaty section in which the early key concept of cognitive analytic therapy, that of ‘Traps’, ‘Snags’ and ‘Dilemmas’ is outlined. ‘Traps’, ‘Snags’ and ‘Dilemmas’ are self-repeating, repetitively deployed maladaptive sequences of thinking, feeling and acting. Ostensibly these sequences are attempting to satisfy an aim but, in fact, for various reasons they only reinforce themselves and preclude more helpful ways of going about things. It was an insight of early CAT therapy that these repetitive patterns were not usually deployed because the patient wished to fail repeatedly, nor were they deployed because of some unconscious psychodynamically driven aim but, instead, were repeatedly deployed because there was no check built into them to see whether the outcomes had been satisfactory. Cognitive analytic therapy was committed to the idea that sustained joint attention between therapist and patient could help the patient become aware of the way in which their patterns were not helping them and, then, begin to make changes using what Vygotsky and other Russian psychologists of that era called ‘Higher Functions’. Thus, a bottom-up understanding of why things were going wrong was combined with a top-down view of change in therapy. It is this top-down perspective on change techniques that makes CAT a particularly apt therapy for a self-help book. The second section of Change for the Better helps the patient to use some of the tools which might well be deployed during cognitive analytic therapy - gathering information and using writing about the ‘self’ to make a programme of change, and then enacting it.

Psychoanalytic Inquiry23(3), 412-59, 2003

The Developmental Roots of Borderline Personality Disorder in Early Attachment Relationships: A Theory and Some Evidence

Peter Fonagy, Mary Target, George Gergely, Jon G. Allen and Anthony W. Bateman

The paper suggests a way of understanding borderline personality disorder in terms of the failure of a secure base. We begin with an account of optimal self-development in a secure attachment context, highlighting the importance of the caregiver's ability to help the small child think about his own and others' minds. This optimal self-development is crucial in developing the child's capacity for mentalization, which can enhance his resilience in the face of later trauma. We discuss the impact of attachment trauma in later development, arguing that the extent of this impact depends on how well early attachment relationships facilitated the capacity for mentalization. We identify some of the consequences for the representations of the internal world of a failure of mentalization that may follow trauma in individuals made vulnerable by genetic predisposition or disorganized early attachment. We link these features to the clinical presentation associated with borderline personality organization. Finally, some of the necessary characteristics of successful psychotherapeutic treatment of borderline personality are briefly considered.



Sexual and Relationship Therapy18(3), 309-28, 2003

The Anatomy of Arousal: Three Internet Portals

Patrick J. Carnes

Internet sexual behaviour offers a unique opportunity to understand processes which influence arousal. This paper studies the Internet as a source of accelerated perception for researchers by examining three different genres of Internet behaviour: ‘Lolita’ sites, ‘chick trick’ sites and ‘granny’ sites. Across all three sites are examples of stimulation that result in compulsive cycles, risk to participants and unique patterns of arousal without previous precedent. All three examples share commonalities that have implications for both researchers and therapists. Specific recommendations for clinical intervention and further research are made.

Defensive Processes Enacted through Mountaineering and Their Impact on Climbers

Pat Hunt and Brian Daines

Brian Daines

NG7 2RD. [emails: Pat.Hunt@nottingham.ac.uk and brian.share@virgin.net]

Brian Daines  

This paper looks at the split-off nature of climbing for those who practise extreme mountaineering, and for whom climbing is a way of life. The regressive processes and idealization involved in this are explored. In particular, the breakdown of idealization at the point where the possibility of death has to be faced is discussed. The impact on close relationship is outlined and conclusions drawn about the main underlying object-relation processes operating in climbers.

Questioning Unspoken Suppositions

Alec McGuire

Alec McGuire

34 Gledhow Wood Road, Leeds LS8 4BZ. [email: ajmcg@tiscali.co.uk]

Alec McGuire  

Dear Editor

The responses to the letters from James Taylor and me about Harold Bourne's article ‘A homosexual turns to women’ (BJP 19(4), June 2003) have included the assertion that we wish to censor debate. But actually, seeking to question unspoken suppositions is of the essence of honest discussion. In our letters, we contested the bases of Bourne's writing, and, in particular, the apparent assumption that lesbian and gay sexual identity is inherently a sign of pathology. It is notable that the responses to our letters have not significantly addressed this issue.

The assertion that a particular identity is pathological has substantial implications for the lives of the individuals concerned, which makes it reasonable to want to know the grounds for the assertion. For lesbians and gay men, apart from the reinforcement of general social homophobia, there are the historically well-evidenced issues of questionable medical and psychotherapeutic treatment, of a tradition of exclusion from the psychotherapy profession, and of the reinforcement of negative self-esteem by introjecting the psychotherapist's beliefs, amongst other things. If the attitudes and beliefs of psychotherapists concerning same-sex orientation turn out to rest on no sustainable evidential base, then psychotherapy has much to answer for. It's ironic that what ought to be the most self-examined of professions is sometimes very reluctant indeed to look at its own assumptions.

The principle that only heterosexual identity is healthy usually turns out, on examination, to consist in little more than the assertion that it is ‘natural’. Such a proposition is unavoidably circular. It says that something is natural because it is natural. It provides no ground for believing it other than its own authority, sidesteps all need to justify itself, and doesn't allow that reality might be more complicated.

Actually, it's those who think thus who turn out to be undertaking whatever censorship may be going on. The overwhelming tenor of recent research in the fields of experimental psychology, genetics, sociology, anthropology, ethology and animal studies has been in two complementary directions, tending to show both that the expression of sexuality is highly socially influenced, and also that same-sex sexuality has a strong innate element that extends beyond the human species to include a wide range of other animals in which same-sex bonding, including life-long partnership, can be seen consistently to occur. If psychotherapy just ignores all this, it can hardly claim to care about possessing a scientific base.

Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy17(4), 300-311, 2003

Thirty Years of Abdominal Pain

Julian Stern

In this paper, the author describes a brief psychotherapy with a man who has struggled with abdominal symptoms for most of his adult life. After an unhappy childhood, the patient (Mr A) married and then was witness to the birth of his stillborn child, in a foreign country. Soon after his abdominal symptoms started, and plagued him for the following 30 years. In the therapy, Mr A began to explore areas of guilt, hostility, and shame, together with previously unknown-about unconscious phantasies. By the end of the therapy, he reported a substantial diminution in his symptoms, as well as changes to his relationships, and mode of thinking and feeling. Some aspects of working psychoanalytically with patients with somatic symptoms, especially those pertaining to the gastrointestinal tract are discussed.



Psychoanalytic Inquiry23(5), 646-677, 2003

Vulnerability, Affect, and Depth in Group Psychotherapy

Martin S. Livingston

This paper describes the importance of a clinical focus on affect and narcissistic vulnerability in the deepening of therapeutic process. An experience of the analyst's emotional availability and understanding is also essential to mutative change. The case material illustrates how such a focus, within a relational context that includes the analyst's own vulnerability, can lead to change.



Psychoanalytic Inquiry23(5), 734-749, 2003

How Group Analysis Cures: An Exploration of Narcissistic Rage in Group Treatment

Christine C. Kieffer

This paper addresses the use of group analysis in treating individuals for whom chronic narcissistic rage is a prominent feature of their character. Such individuals are often especially suspicious of participating in group experiences, as their sensitivity to slight and circumscribed empathy for others often leaves them vulnerable to being attacked and ostracized in groups. Their history often reveals experiences in which they were either the scapegoat of the family or of the playground, often both. Such individuals, however, may also long for inclusion and acceptance, and thus participation in a therapeutic group may be a particularly important part of their continued development. An extended clinical vignette illustrates how such work occurs within a therapeutic group using a self-psychological mode. Narcissistic rage as manifested within the group-as-a-whole or groupself is also examined.

Sabina Spielrein: Forgotten Pioneer of Psychoanalysis edited by Coline Covington and Barbara Wharton. Published by Brunner-Routledge, Hove and New York, 2003; 305 pp; £30.00 hardback.

Susan Budd

Susan Budd

British Psychoanalytical Society, London

Susan Budd  

Sabina Spielrein, a young woman from Rostov-on-Don, the daughter of a wealthy businessman, was brought by her uncle to the Burghölzli Clinic in Zürich in 1904. She was 19 years old and a highly intelligent, troublesome hysteric who had been brought to Switzerland for cure. There she met Carl Gustav Jung, who had recently become a member of the staff of the Clinic and, together with his new wife, had an apartment there. He had read some of Freud's work, and was keen to try out psychoanalysis with his gifted young patient. Sabina's fate has been that, until recently, she ‘is perhaps best known for her love affair with Carl Jung’ (p. 1). Her illness and recovery were powerfully represented in a recent play, Christopher Hampton's The Talking Cure, which showed, with a certain amount of dramatic licence, how she became first a link and then a source of friction between the two men.

The publication of this book represents years of work, negotiation and patient waiting on the part of the editors. Various chapters have had to be translated at various times from German, French, Italian and Russian. Sabina's hospital records from the Burghölzli had to be released by her descendents. Her diary and her correspondence with both Freud and Jung were discovered in a cardboard box in 1977, during the restoration of a palace in Geneva which had previously been the Psychological Institute. Their significance was recognized by Aldo Carotenuto, a Jungian analyst. Knowledge of the love affair immediately brought Sabina to prominence; before then, as Sabine Richebacher points out, ‘she was represented in the psychoanalytic literature by four footnotes in the works of Freud’.

Since 1980, there has been much greater interest in Sabina's life and her role in the lives of Jung and Freud, but relatively little in her own work; she published over 30 papers, and seems to have been actively interested in child analysis and the earliest stages of psychic development after the birth of her daughter in 1913. One of her papers, ‘The origin of the child's words Papa and Mama: some observations on the different stages in language development’ (1922), is reproduced here. It is of genuine continuing interest; it discusses whether the child seeks language or invents it, and picks up on the questions of the origins of language which has been almost a Russian prerogative; ‘the ancestor sleeps within the child, and the child within the ancestor’ (p. 291). She argues that verbal language is social, designed for communication, but that prior to this there are earlier languages - the autistic and the magical. The first sounds are produced by, and therefore come to hallucinate, the action of sucking; ‘mama’ conjures up the feeding breast.

F***ing, Failing and Finding Out (Disgrace by J.M. Coetzee, Secker & Warburg, London, 1999)

Herb Hahn

Herb Hahn

London

Herb Hahn  

In arranging for David Laurie and Melanie Isaacs to have sex, J.M. Coetzee produces the embryo of his stark and gripping yarn. It develops, like a good analysis, by unexpected twists and turns, many of them painful. As readers, we accompany Professor Laurie as he stumbles, tumbles and falls into the swirling currents and eddies of present-day South Africa. Eventually he surfaces, stranded, broke and defaced (literally) and gives up hope of completing his last remaining project: an opera about Byron and unrequited love. He is now prepared to settle for something infinitely more modest: ‘That somewhere from amidst the welter of sound there will - like a bird - dart up a single authentic note of immortal longing’.

Coetzee's plot has the protagonist, a scholar of Wordsworth and one-time professor of English literature, being sacked in disgrace. This is just the beginning of his journey into and through hell until he eventually reaches a kind of salvation. When Laurie retreats from his university town seeking at least temporary sanctuary with his daughter Lucy on her country smallholding, he is not at all prepared for his agonizing helplessness and humiliation when his beloved only child is gang-raped. To make matters even worse for him, Lucy and he fall out when she determines to sit out the disgrace of her ensuing pregnancy. He nevertheless feels an obligation to be on standby and rents a basic room in the nearby village to sleep in while he bases himself at the bare clinic run by Bev Shaw. Here he chooses to slave away unpaid for seven days a week assisting Bev to treat and put down unwanted dogs and other animals. Finally he sacrifices the only being (a lame dog, also representing himself) with which he has the most meaningful, remaining mutual attachment.

For the unalienated reader, Coetzee's message may seem to be that there is more, qualitatively more, to discovering meaning in the hum an imal condition than being a privileged, clever, elegantly articulate, committed scholar of dead poets. In fact his flawed protagonist is shown to be oedipally stuck, desiring and sleeping with an endless series of very young women. An outcome of the process of his disgrace and torment is that it also provides him with an opportunity to internalize a good enough father figure in the morally anchored, family oriented, dedicated village schoolmaster, who is also Melanie's father. And Bev Shaw who devotedly and compassionately runs the clinic for sick, suffering and abandoned animals provides Laurie with the basis of a new kind of maternal introject. Thus, inspired and spiritually awakened, he begins to discover new meaning in his life.

Wendy Bratherton

Cambridge

Wendy Bratherton  

Most counsellors, psychotherapists and analysts will, at some time or other, work with people who self-harm. Yet there has not been, to my knowledge, such a comprehensive study of the literature on the topic. Fiona Gardner goes some way to rectifying this in her book entitled Self-Harm: A Psychotherapeutic Approach.

Her main aim in the book is to unravel the different meanings behind the act, usually cutting, which leads to self-harm. In our culture today this is prevalent among young people, and so her clinical focus is on those between the ages of 15 and 21, who are prone to cutting repeatedly. These are predominantly girls. She draws on her many years of experience of working with those who self-harm both as a social worker in social services and family guidance, and as a psychoanalytical psychotherapist in voluntary organizations, a public sector clinic and in private practice.

Later Reflections on the Paper

Josephine Klein

Josephine Klein

Josephine Klein  

‘Patients not ready for interpretation’ was the topic I was puzzling over more than any other, 20 years ago. Why weren't they ready? What is ‘ready’? Should we persist in interpreting, or adapt to their ways? For me the topic seemed an important one at that time. What has changed since then, in our attitudes and our practice?

I was thrilled when I learned that my paper on this topic was to be included in the commemorative issue of the BJP. But re-reading gave me a shock - nothing to do with the main issues, but how I now regret my accounts of ‘Rose’ and ‘Ken’! Like many others, I now think we not should indulge in these general accounts, brief or lengthy, even when ‘Rose’ and ‘Ken’ agree to them, unless there is some precisely formulated reason for them. In this paper they do not further the argument in any precise way.

I am now also embarrassed to note how little I trusted the common sense of BJP readers - how I conscientiously spelled out some obvious considerations! Or was that necessary 15 years ago?

But I think the paper does retain some merits. There are, alas, still many psychoanalytically-oriented psychotherapists whom I like and respect, to whom I rarely refer prospective patients because I fear they might regard them not primarily as suffering people but primarily as people likely to be devious, stubborn and self-deceiving, with a major interest in outwitting their therapist. While I agree that ‘the heart is deceitful and desperately wicked’, and that many patients need at times to be managed by having their evasive manoeuvres interpreted, nevertheless it still seems to me counterproductive to react to these manoeuvres as moral flaws rather than defences against pain. There are still therapists with this attitude, though fewer, I think. I do not think that an editor of the BJP would now write (as one did in 1990), that this paper is about ‘patients who stubbornly refuse to accept their unconscious motives and phantasies’ (my italics). At that time, few who read the editorial noticed the condemnatory tone, even though the very title of the paper proposed that there were people who were simply not ready, not disobliging or stubborn - just not ready.

Margaret Arden

50 Highlands Heath, Portsmouth Road, Putney, London SW15 3TX. [email: ardenml@waitrose.com]

Margaret Arden  

In this paper the history of consciousness will be discussed in relation to the place of psychoanalysis in the history of ideas. A holistic way of thinking is described, which brings together various ideas about how the nature of reality is perceived, when science has for the last 200 years seemed to win out over religion. The influence of Goethe on Freud suggests an unrecognized holistic element in Freud's work. A holistic approach reconciles some of the divisions between scientific and religious thinking and leads to a discussion of the sacred.

Celia Harding

Celia Harding

London

Celia Harding  

This thought-provoking series of papers challenges complacency towards ethical matters. In his Foreword, Lord Alderdice writes ‘Ethical practice means something more and quite different from not falling foul of the code of ethics and practice’ (p. vii). The ‘ethical attitude’, elaborated in the book, is what is ‘more’ and ‘quite different’.

Contributors from various theoretical backgrounds (weighted by Jungian, Analytical Psychologists) agree that an ethical attitude is embedded in analytic work. In their introduction, Mary Twyman and Hester McFarland Solomon describe the ethical attitude as the ‘structure and ballast’, sustaining the analytic attitude through the creative and destructive storms unleashed in the analytic process. Essential to the analytic attitude are an open and receptive mind, refraining from re-active or retaliatory responses, dedicated to finding meaning and value in the patient's communications. An ethical attitude and good analytic practice are two sides of one coin. Without the ethical attitude the analytic space collapses.

For Twyman the ethical attitude is captured in a form of unconditional responsibility. McFarland Solomon locates this responsibility in a developmental perspective, which translates into the analyst's ‘thoughtful devotedness’ towards the patient, their analytic relationship and work together. The ethical attitude seeks to recognize, discover and facilitate the development of the patient as an individual rather than as an extension of the analyst. This endeavour depends on the analyst's openness both to themselves and their patient and on their willingness to become subject to the analytic process. The analytic space has the potential to transform both parties to the relationship.

Georgia Lepper  

This learning pack consists of a video recording of John Woods's three part dramatization of a generational case history, ‘The End of Abuse’: A Play Reading in Three Parts, accompanied by a copy of the text, including a foreword by Estela Welldon, and an epilogue by John Woods. A third important component of the pack is a set of clinical commentaries, from a variety of clinicians, all of whom are informed by and work within the International Attachment Network. Each part of the pack represents a substantial piece of work and therefore deserves its own comment, so I will begin with some comments on the elements which make up this piece of work. Then I will move on to some thoughts about its impact as a training tool for psychotherapists. Finally, I will consider The End of Abuse in the wider context of mental health training needs.

The play is based on John Woods's own case experience, but not on any specific case: it is a representation of ‘caseness’ (by which I mean the set of professional practices, categorizations and decisions by which a life story is transformed into a case history).

Introduction

Dorothy Hamilton

Dorothy Hamilton

c/o AGIP, 1 Fairbridge Road, London N19 3EW. [email: dorothyh@ntlworld.com]

Dorothy Hamilton  

Our work as analytical psychotherapists has to do precisely with the exploration of subjectivity, and consciousness might be said to be our primary tool. We may look ideally placed to speak of its nature. But at a time when consciousness is everywhere under discussion, it is little spoken of as a phenomenon in our own field: we seem still to take it for granted, as until recently it has been elsewhere. In David Black's metaphor, it is the primary task of the therapist to attend to the lamp and the lamp-stand, not to the light as such. And indeed, it could be pointed out that the central focus of our work is with the unconscious; but when we say that our task is to bring the as yet unknown to consciousness, to what, exactly, are we bringing it? This is the area AGIP set out, somewhat ambitiously, to explore in our series of conferences on ‘The Nature of Consciousness and its Relation to Psychoanalysis’.*

At the time, we scarcely realized how ambitious. The meaning of the word ‘consciousness’, as we were to discover, becomes the more elusive the more you consider it. And no wonder, for as the writers published here tell us in their different ways, it is not actually possible for consciousness - in its essence a subjective experience - reflexively to consider itself in any ‘scientific’ way as an object. David Black says: ‘There is no way that science can explain consciousness, because consciousness is what knows science, consciousness is logically anterior to science’. And Warren Colman quotes Laing: ‘The truth that I am trying to grasp is the grasp that is trying to grasp it’. ‘I can never reach the edge of my consciousness’, says Colman; as he shows it to us, it is effectively infinite.

Or is it rather, as Joseph Schwartz suggests, infinitesimal: a non-problem, a mere and minor ray of light on the overwhelming vastness of the unconscious?

Long-Term Outcome of Long-Term Psychoanalytically Oriented Therapies: First Findings of the Stockholm Outcome of Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis Study

Johan Blomberg, Anna Lazar and Rolf Sandell

The scarcity of findings on the effectiveness of psychodynamic long-term psychotherapy and psychoanalysis is a problem, at least in countries where these treatments are the general treatment of choice. In this study, a sample of 405 patients in various stages before, during, and after treatment was drawn from a population of 1,200 patients who had received or were on a waiting list for public subsidized long-term psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapy or psychoanalysis. The average duration was 40 months for the psychotherapies and 51 months for the psychoanalyses. All patients completed a questionnaire, including the Symptom Checklist-90 (SCL-90), Sense of Coherence Scale (SOCS), and Social Adjustment Scale (SAS), on 3 occasions with 12-month intervals. Using a partly within- and between-subjects design, group means were regressed on an ordinal time scale covering 7 stages in the treatment process: before, early during, during, late during, soon after, after, and late after treatment. The slopes indicated small to moderate effect sizes (d = 0.4-0.6) for psychotherapy and moderate to very large effect sizes (d = 0.4-1.5) for psychoanalysis. The largest effect sizes were on the SCL-90 and the lowest on the SAS for both groups. The proportions of patients with more ‘healthy’ scores compared with the worst scoring 10% in a nonclinical norm group increased from roughly 30% to 55% in the psychotherapy group and from 10% to 75% in the psychoanalysis group. The results underscore the importance of long-term follow-up when evaluation of long-term treatments is concerned.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis82, 1105-21, 2001

The Teaching of the Oedipus Complex: On Making Freud Meaningful to University Students by Unveiling His Essential Ideas on the Human Condition

Rachel B. Blass

The author describes an approach that she has developed to the teaching of Freud's Oedipus complex to university psychology students (both graduates and undergraduates). The approach is based on the notion that Freud's theories become meaningful to students when they can find in them important and interesting statements regarding the human condition, and when they see that they can use these statements to gain a more in-depth understanding of seemingly simple concrete life circumstances and events. In the course of this description the author focuses on two basic statements that are embedded within Freud's comments on the male Oedipus complex. These statements go beyond simple portrayals of the Oedipus complex as founded on castration anxiety and pertain to love and fear and how we grow in our attempts to deal with their inherently conflictual nature. This approach entails a shift away from more schematic and distant forms of teaching the Oedipus complex as well as other aspects of psychoanalytic theory that are common and problematic in universities today.

Consciousness, the Self and the Isness Business

Warren Colman

Warren Colman

16 Chequer Street, St Albans, Herts AL1 3YD. [email: wgc.net2mail@ntlworld.com]

Warren Colman  

This paper considers consciousness from the point of view of extreme materialism, which asserts that everything is physical and extreme idealism, which asserts that ‘the world is my idea’. Attempting to avoid dualism, I argue that there is no fundamental ground of being and that consciousness is a no-thing. Science can explain its mechanisms in terms of ‘propositional knowledge’ but this is distinct from the ‘experiential knowledge’ that refers to the domain of meaning (psychic reality). Although consciousness is omnipresent and infinite, it is surrounded by the further infinity of the Unknown. Together these comprise the totality that Jung called ‘the Self’. The paper concludes with some reflections on the experience of Being in ‘the Isness Business’.

Bob Hinshelwood

373 Smeeth Road, Marshland St James, Nr Wisbech, Cambridgeshire PE14 8EP. [email: bob@hinsh.freeserve.co.uk]

Bob Hinshelwood  

This is a retrospective issue. It is about development, about change. It is about the change in us, in psychotherapy itself. In her editorial, Rachel refers to ‘fine fat fish’, some that were included in this issue, some that got away. What is a fat fish today? Is it the same as yesterday? The selection here surely must be a mirror reflection of today's preoccupations as much as it is an accurate picture of 20 years ago.

This issue is also to celebrate the Journal's achievement. What is that achievement?

One immediate success was that in 1984 half-a-dozen apparently warring groups sat down with me, calmly to work out our cooperative venture. All that divisiveness from the 1970s seemed to have another side to it - a willingness to cooperate that had been frustrated until I blundered along to suggest it.

With that in mind, it seemed to me we needed a Journal that was a mouthpiece for all sorts of voices in our world - not just an up-to-the-minute account of the latest ideas, but a vehicle for the expression of the political ambitions and anxieties. In those days, when we started the Journal, there was a forlorn sense of the endless quarrels and the compulsively divisive nature of psychotherapy organizations. It was a crazy-paving landscape. ‘It was an injured eagle’. We needed therapy.

I wrote in my first Editorial:

There should have been a Journal for Psychotherapists a long time ago. One can only speculate on the reasons why we have not had one. It must be to do with the fragmented state of the profession … All this separateness creates group dynamics within the profession that polarizes individuals and organizations into positions increasingly distant from each other … However the appearance of this Journal is not a miraculous circus act, juggling all the disparate influences into one swaying edifice of acrobats. It comes at a time when there is suddenly a wide recognition of the need to establish some common principles … This willingness appears in other activities as well - for instance, the ‘Rugby’ Conference.

Introduction

Jan Lee

Jan Lee

85 Speldhurst Road, Chiswick, London W4 1BY. [email: jslvoyages@aol.com]

Jan Lee  

The history of brief therapy is as long as the history of psychotherapy itself. Freud, Jung, Klein, Winnicott and many other influential analysts all saw patients for short periods of time on contracts that varied in degree of clarity and structure. This practice was not seen as anything remarkable. Psychotherapy itself was still an inchoate field and brief therapy was not as yet defined as a particular strand amidst many new developments. In Britain brief therapy began to emerge as a separate discipline due to the ground-breaking work of Balint and Malan in the focal therapy workshops begun at the Tavistock during the 1950s. As their research into time-limited work became increasingly impressive, brief therapy began to develop as a specific area of expertise with its own issues, techniques and theories. Different models of brief therapy have since appeared representing almost every avenue of psychotherapeutic thought.

It seemed apposite to revisit brief therapy practices in this section, given that the last decade has seen a proliferation of time-limited work in public and private settings. Primarily a reflection of changing socio-economic forces and managerial fashions in mental health provision, this packaging and greater consumption of psychotherapy as a product may be seen either as a dumbing down or as a growing recognition of its usefulness, albeit in abridged form. Clearly brief therapy has arrived and is here to stay. But how do patients and psychotherapists feel about it?

The section explores this question, beginning with Clinical Commentary XXIII, which contains four pieces, and finishing with a paper by Anna Bravesmith in which she presents her brief work in a primary care setting, followed by a theoretical discussion. In the traditional format of the Clinical Commentary Section, authors are asked to write about an anonymous vignette. These provide a glimpse into the work of the therapeutic dyad but leave the psychotherapist without a voice. So, in a departure from the usual format, the authors here were asked to offer examples from their own clinical work and to write the commentary on this material themselves. This device was adopted to allow some freedom of expression about the experience of brief therapy from the psychotherapist's chair.

Sari Ferber

Sari Ferber

Haifa 31905, Israel. [email: sarig@research.haifa.ac.il]

Sari Ferber  

The phenomenon of silence in therapy has not elicited a great deal of research in the past 50 years, but cases that were published acknowledged the many facets of silence in therapy and its having a communicative function and being part of the transference. The aim of this article is to demonstrate a case in which a patient exhibited different kinds of silences which stemmed from different sources over the course of nine years of psychotherapy. In analysing the case, it was proposed that the patient used silences in order to attain proximity to the therapist as an attachment figure and to base the proximity and distance in relation to her. It was also proposed that his silences matured and developed from expressing avoidance to the expression of intimacy thus facilitating the maturation of his capacity to maintain a dialogue. The possibility of interpreting silences is discussed in terms of attachment theory.

Worrying Developments in Europe

Haya Oakley

Haya Oakley

London [email: hayaoakley@freenetname.co.uk]

Haya Oakley  

Dear Editor

I wish to widen the terms of the debate about The College of Psychoanalysts - United Kingdom started in the BJP (20(3)), in the light of recent worrying developments in Europe.

The background is that on 11 February 2004 the European Commission decided to add psychotherapy to the list of professions for which it issues directives. European training standards and ethical guidelines will be decided in Brussels and will be applied in all member states enabling members of professions to practise throughout the EU.

The European Association of Psychotherapists (EAP) and UKCP are pleased with the EC decision because Brussels apparently promised to base the directive on the European Certificate for Psychotherapy (ECP) promoted by the EAP and awarded in the UK by UKCP. The ECP is constituted under the laws of Austria, the only country in continental Europe which defines psychotherapy not as a form of medical treatment to be practised only by psychiatrists and some psychologists but as an independent ‘psycho-social activity’. The ECP requires a first degree in a ‘health profession’ but will accept equivalence.

However, in France, an amendment has been introduced to an ancient law designed to protect the public from gypsies and cults, defining psychotherapy as a ‘medical treatment’ which may be practised only by physicians and those in possession of a degree in clinical psychology. The rationale was that up to one third of the 30,000 practitioners of psychotherapy in France were viewed as working in ‘cults’ and that special regulations must be put in place to protect the public from them.

Louise Lyon

Louise Lyon

Adolescent Department, Tavistock Clinic, Tavistock and Portman NHS Trust, 120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA

Louise Lyon  

The Young People's Consultation Service (YPCS) was set up in 1961 by the Youth Studies and Research Foundation which itself was one of a number of projects financed by a Dutch charitable foundation. It was initially based in a non-institutional building and staffed by psychoanalytically trained psychologists and social workers. The founders proposed a service

independent of the adolescent's world of authority, to which young people may come and discuss their immediate problems without any need for a deep or permanent relationship being created … The adolescents, by discussion with well-trained advisers, can work out their own problems and attain insight into them so that they may return to their milieu and make growth and progress.

In 1967 the service transferred to the NHS and found a home in the Adolescent Department of the Tavistock Clinic, Tavistock and Portman NHS Trust, London.

The YPCS accepts self-referrals only and offers up to four weekly therapeutic consultation sessions to people aged 16 to 30 who have a personal or emotional problem they feel they would like to talk about. The four therapeutic consultations aim to encourage a process of self-discovery rather than dependency.

Clinical Material

When Ms A, a 23-year-old white woman, contacted the YPCS, she told the administrator that she felt low all the time and lacked motivation. Over the first three sessions I learned that she was about to start a permanent job, having been temping and travelling for two years. She described having experienced lengthy periods of depression which she felt she had only recognized recently. Her depression was presented as inevitable because her father and elder brother were both chronically depressed. She had felt obliged to be a bright and lively child to make up for her brother's failure to make a success of his life but this in turn provoked his envy and jealousy.

LOUISE LYON is Chair of Young People's Consultation Service, consultant clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst. Address for correspondence: Adolescent Department, Tavistock Clinic, Tavistock and Portman NHS Trust, 120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA.

The Concept of the Death Instinct: A Clinical Viewpoint

Dear Editor

I read with interest David M. Black's review of the concept and the commentary by Joseph Schwartz (Black 2001; Schwartz 2001). Although the Editorial Board have indicated that they will invite further response to this debate in future issues, it was a pity that a commentary was not sought that provided a contrasting view, to encourage the reader to form their own conclusions.

Both Black and Schwartz argue their case at a metapsychological level, questioning the way through which Freud first introduced the concept. Black, as a result, concludes that ‘the death drive, as such, probably merits no future in psychoanalytic thinking’.

Schwartz fully endorses Black's conclusion, saying that ‘we should stop thinking in terms of a death drive but directly in terms of destructiveness’ and, forcibly, adds that ‘we should stop teaching the death drive in our trainings’. However, Schwartz enigmatically ends his article with ‘And so we come to clinical cases’. Yet, what is striking in both the critique by Black and the endorsing commentary by Schwartz is indeed the absence of any clinical material to support their thesis of abandoning the death instinct.

Laplanche and Pontalis (1973) point out in their detailed review of the death instinct that a dualistic tendency is fundamental to Freudian thought. The introduction of the death instinct added another dimension when confronted with the ambivalent nature of communications from people in very disturbed states of mind. This is aside from considering its operation as a universal phenomenon.

The theoretical value of the concept in understanding clinical phenomena perhaps explains why Freud should end up writing so strongly to endorse the notion from its original speculative foundations. He writes:

To begin with, it was only tentatively that I put forward the views that I have developed here, but in the course of time they have gained such a hold upon me that I can no longer think in any other way. (Freud 1930, p. 119)

As a practising general psychiatrist, I find that I can no longer think in any other way than as described above by Freud, when relating to patients with major psychotic disorders. In schizophrenia, Bion (1957) drew our attention to the never decided conflict between the life and death instincts as the dominating feature throughout the patient's life.

Julian Leff

Julian Leff

Department of Psychiatry, University College and Royal Free Hospital Medical School, London

Julian Leff  

Is a language needed for communication between people with psychosis and their carers, both professional and non-professional? If so, does there need to be one language or several? The answer to this question is determined partly by the unusual experiences of people with psychotic illnesses. Many of them are not shared with the general public and therefore language has not developed to encompass them. There is of course a professional vocabulary to describe these experiences, for instance ‘delusions’ and ‘hallucinations’, but these terms are not in common usage so are only taken up by patients who learn them from the professionals. Some patients develop their own words to stand for their unvoiced experiences, creative extensions of language known technically as neologisms. For example, a patient of mine referred to his auditory hallucinations as ‘acousticals’. Others employ words in everyday usage but juxtapose them in apparently illogical nonsensical sequences. A patient produced the following speech: ‘I didn't do this properly and I got thrown out of jail by super-bails, cricketer's bails, sir, Normans. Do you know Normans? Roses and R.C.s and E.C.s. Inch prisms and Canterbury bells’.

This seeming random association of words becomes meaningful when we know his recent history. He was arrested and put in prison in Canterbury, from whence he was bailed out by a friend of his named Norman. Without the illumination of the factual story the patient was attempting to convey, his utterances could easily be dismissed as nonsense. The same is true of delusions and hallucinations, which are often treated by professional and non-professional carers alike as the nonsensical products of a diseased mind. But they do not originate in the chaos of psychosis even if they are transformed by it. They have their roots in real experiences, of events and emotional states, sometimes dating back to the patient's early years. A particular kind of listening is required to decipher the language of psychosis into the common tongue of human experience. Possessing the skill for this taxing form of translation is not by itself sufficient. In order to share that understanding with the patient, it is necessary to find words that will resonate with the patient while in the throes of psychosis.

Chris MacKenna

Chris MacKenna

London

Chris MacKenna  

This is an original and thought-provoking book which deserves to be widely read, pondered on and discussed. The subtitle gets it right: Josephine Klein has given us 11 more or less free-standing essays which lay the groundwork for an exploration of the ineffable within the context of contemporary psychotherapy.

The book is addressed to mental health professionals generally, but perhaps particularly - given the body of theory on which it draws - to analytically oriented psychotherapists and counsellors who are interested in thinking about experiences of ‘love, wonder, awe, joy, inspiration, and particularly the feelings that seem to give us a sense that there is something beyond what we can easily find words for - ineffable feelings’ (pp. 1 f.). Numinous feelings are ‘not so very rare’ yet, Klein feels, they:

are not normally regarded in the consulting-room - unless they can be called psychotic … Their exclusion shows also in the lack of reference to them in the indices of the International Journal of Psychoanalysis and other mainstream psychotherapy journals - no mention there of awe, worship, numen, devotion, etc. Yet these feelings exist and are presumably at times felt and spoken about in psychotherapeutic sessions. Alas, perhaps we stare out of countenance the feelings that do not fit easily into the theories we have so far constructed. (pp. 75 f.)

This is fighting talk, but Klein presses the point. Discussing the adjective ‘blithe’, with its cognate meanings of ‘jocund, gay, sprightly, merry, joyous, cheerful, glad, happy, well’, she comments:

At the time of writing … psychotherapists are tending to ignore expressions of such positive feelings in the expectation that they cover other feelings, thought to be more genuine, of depression and anger. Are those psychotherapists always right about this, or are they projecting their own experiences of darkness on to a world that, whatever its appalling atrocities and occasional preference for dreariness, is yet at many moments cheerier than they can perceive? (pp. 127 f.)

Jean Knox  

This book offers an original perspective on the study of the feminine, exploring Jungian models of gender in relation to Lacanian and post-Lacanian concepts. The editors and authors have thus undertaken a difficult and ambitious project in that both classical Jungian and Lacanian theory can be interpreted as denigratory in their attitude to women and to the feminine psyche, and would also seem to exist at almost opposite poles of the spectrum of analytic theory. This book immediately involves the reader in the challenging task of finding new insights that might succeed in integrating these disparate positions. The two co-editors, Tessa Adams and Andrea Duncan, each offer three chapters, and there are individual chapters by Shirley Wheeley (who sadly died shortly after completing her contribution), Marie Angelo, Margaret Clark and Joy Schaverien. The authors therefore provide a mix of clinical and academic approaches to their chosen field.

This book invites psychotherapists of all theoretical orientations who do not draw significantly on Lacanian ideas to reconsider that position. One crucial question that recurs to the reader throughout this book is whether he or she accepts the Lacanian thesis that the law of the father is enshrined in the ‘symbolic order’ - language itself. The centrality of a Lacanian model for all the authors of this book is exemplified and succinctly summarized in the chapter by Schaverien, who investigates the implications for women of Lacan's view that it is phallic qualities which initiate difference and that it is in the name of the father that we must recognize the support of the symbolic function.

The Future of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy edited by Lucy King and Rosemary Randall. Published by Whurr, London, 2003; 230 pages; £25.00 paperback.

Fiona Gardner

Fiona Gardner

Bristol

Fiona Gardner  

I remember one of the founders of my own training suggesting that there are two ways to nurture the development of psychoanalytic psychotherapy students and also presumably qualified professionals. She likened the process to growing roses: one results in a line of espalier roses, their growth firmly directed and trained against the wall. The other leads to lots of bushes of different sizes and shapes growing into their own potential. It is clear from this collection of papers largely produced by those connected to the Cambridge Society of Psychotherapy that the ethos is of the ‘let a thousand flowers bloom’ school of thought. As far as the book goes this leads to a mixed bunch, with some bright flowers and some where drastic pruning could have helped.

The CSP editors Lucy King and Rosemary Randall in their inviting introduction to this book suggest that psychoanalytic psychotherapy finds itself between a rock and a hard place. On the one hand, it is subject to the same criticisms as psychoanalysis, criticisms about a lack of scientific credibility or low-cost effectiveness, or that treatment is prolonged for economic self-interest with little proof of success. On the other hand, the expansion of psychoanalytic ideas seems to be disapproved of by established and élitist psychoanalytic institutes who want to keep control. The editors seek to look at the value of ‘hybrid vigour: the creative potential released when the “dire mastery” of psychoanalytic tradition and succession is put aside’ (p. xii). To do this they write that much of the book is concerned with those who speak from the margins but who are neglected as contributing to the profession. As a second major theme King and Randall comment on the managerial and accountability pressures that restrict new developments and thinking together with the psychoanalytic psychotherapy organizations' inferiority complex that leads to a hankering after what the editors refer to as the ‘pure gold’ of psychoanalysis.

The 14 chapters of the book are loosely grouped into two halves - the first includes the themes of accountability and legitimacy, and the relationship between psychoanalytic psychotherapy and medical and scientific views of the mind and behaviour. An interesting chapter on psychotherapy as inhabiting an ethical rather than medical domain by Paul Gordon leads into the second half of the collection on issues of cultural and social mores and psychoanalytic psychotherapy practice; and a collection of papers from those whose experiences are often seen as peripheral to psychoanalytic psychotherapy theory and practice. The book ends with a confident chapter ‘Telling it like it is’ by the highly experienced Peter Lomas.

Sexuality and Discourses of Psychotherapy

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

Ann Scott  

From the Editor:

In a recent editorial (BJP 20(1)) I wrote that Harold Bourne's article, ‘A homosexual turns to women’, in the views of two readers, James Taylor and A.J. McGuire, counted as ‘words not in our name’. As James Taylor wrote: ‘Unless offence was intended, an apology might be appropriate; and, at least…. Some kind of explanation to the readership’.

We've considered the request for an apology for publication of the article at the Editorial Board and concluded that an apology from the Journal is not needed. This is essentially because we see Bourne's article as promoting debate. We recognize that his view of homosexuality may not be shared by others, but we think such differences of view should be debated. Board members and I are respectful of the issues raised by our correspondents, while supporting Harold Bourne's right to argue his own case.

Dr Bourne has effectively answered James Taylor's point about whether the patient consented to the paper being published.

I also recognize the profound difference of idiom between Harold Bourne and his critics, and I want to share some reflections of my own about multiplicities of meaning, focusing on James Taylor's letter. Basing his analysis of Bourne's text on an interesting and productive reading of Foucault and other scholars' work on the formation of general social and psychic categories in relation to dominance/submission and the situation of minorities, Taylor goes on to identify strong and outdated prejudice in Bourne's reading of an individual case. But here there is an assumption about fixity of meaning which in my view can be problematic if the clinical signifiers in the main lead to one conclusion only: homophobia on the part of Harold Bourne. Little remains provisional, or open to more than one interpretation (cf. also Danielle Quinodoz's discussion of ‘a polysemous form of language’ (2003, pp. 1477-8)). Conclusions are hard and fast.

On the other hand, if Bourne's article was, or was experienced as, inflammatory it is not surprising if responses to it are, or are experienced as, inflammatory. The very difficulty in engaging in dialogue about the issues seems to promote a fixity of interpretation in two directions. It is hard to acknowledge the existence of another viewpoint when a single viewpoint is strongly cathected. I still think, however, that it is worth doing. Harold Bourne's writing differs significantly from James Taylor's and A.J. McGuire's - in assumptive framework, literary style, implication and ‘feel’. In that all three writers have found a space within this Journal, however, perhaps they offer further opportunity for dialogue about the complex relationship between intrapsychic development and psychic change, on the one hand; and the dynamics of social and cultural oppression and the psychic legacy of legal marginalization, on the other.

Editorial

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

[annscottbjp@aol.com]

Ann Scott  

This issue of the Journal begins in the external world, with Pat Hunt and Brian Daines' suggestive exploration of the dynamics of climbing. Posing a question about the degree to which these dynamics can be understood within the limits of everyday defensive processes and how much they go beyond this into the clearly pathological, they bring together climbers' written accounts, the ideas of Winnicott, Betty Joseph and Warren Colman, and their own clinical practice to illustrate ideas about the rock as a lover and a holding environment, climbing as a defence against intimacy, and a way of life that can be ‘underpinned by omnipotent denial of mortality’.

Considerations of near-death experience lead into the Journal's Franco-British exchange on sexuality and the death drive, deriving from a joint BJP/Freud Museum conference, ‘Eros and Thanatos’, in 2002. Introduced by Jean Arundale, the papers promote an engagement between key aspects of the conceptual frameworks of Freud, Klein, Bion and Laplanche. Jean Laplanche's and Nicola Abel-Hirsch's papers closely follow their conference presentations. David Bell's commentary on Laplanche, written specially for this issue of the Journal, offers a contemporary Kleinian perspective on the issues. The juxtaposition of these distinct idioms and frameworks allows readers to track similarities and differences, implied or explicit, in conceptions about the origins of the unconscious and processes of binding and unbinding; the nature of perverse sexuality; what sustains the drive for life as well as the vicissitudes of the death drive. Taking just one area as an example: to what extent might Bion's model of a ‘saturated receptor’ (cited in Abel-Hirsch) map onto Laplanche's model of the ‘enigmatic signifier’ in the mother-infant relationship? Bion's focus is on the absence of mother as enabling the first thought; Laplanche's is on the traumatic implantation of messages from the mother. Bell, who welcomes the debate for the opportunity it gives to look at the theoretical work that concepts do, wonders whether Laplanche's model allows a place for the ‘deadening mental anti-life processes’ that contemporary Kleinians are researching.

Introduction and Brief Outline of Some Jungian Concepts

In this paper I endeavour to demonstrate a Jungian approach to dream interpretation by describing the working through of four dreams of an ex-patient whom I shall call Clara.2 I mean a way of working which puts emphasis on the integrating, individuating self, where archetypal imagery is valued and explored and, while early experiences are viewed as important, the focus is not on transference-countertransference (Samuels 1985). In the main body of the paper there will be some background information about the patient but in no way does it attempt to be a case history.

Three of the dreams are referred to as the ‘lion-dreams’. Taking note of the images in her dreams marked the beginning of the patient's psychic work towards individuation, the urge for self-realization and wholeness. This means a development which leads to a mature personality able to cope with and be attuned to both internal and external realities. Ruth Barnett

Ruth Barnett

London

Ruth Barnett  

One of the most important features of literature, both fiction and non-fiction, is that it engenders resonance between the reader and the text. A good book has something important to say and reaches out for dialogue with the reader and her own thoughts and ideas. This book is based on the papers of an academic conference, ‘Trauma and Memory: Cross-Cultural Perspectives’ held at the University of New South Wales in 1998. As such, it will certainly appeal to like-minded scholars and should find its way on to reading lists for cultural and social studies students. The language used by many of the contributors may seem alien to non-academic clinicians so that its pearls may get lost in translation. It may not appeal to a wide readership for this reason as well as the disturbing nature of its subject matter. But it contains much of potential interest for counsellors and psychotherapists.

World Memory is an anthology of 13 essays by 14 writers, seven based in Australia, three in South Africa, three in the USA and one in London, UK. One is an archivist specializing in Aborigines and ‘The Stolen Generation’. One is a poet, writer and former anti-apartheid activist. The other 12 are based in universities. Together they represent the disciplines of art theory, anthropology, education, literature, comparative literature, historiography and psychotherapy. Only three authors are male. Some write as first-hand survivors of trauma and some as second generation. Focusing on memory of trauma is the theme that connects all their essays. Variously they pay their respects and disrespects to Freud and psychoanalysis but this does not figure strongly in the discourse.

World Memory contributes significantly to the topical debate about memory, particularly the contribution of Andreas Huyssen, a scholar of international standing. The approach is mainly philosophical and, because of this, the book contributes to an artificial divide into the science and philosophy of trauma memory. As an anthology it might have done the opposite and created a bridge between the two if it had included some recent work in neurology, psychobiology and psychotherapy research and writings that attempt to find common ground through interaction.

Troubled persons entering psychoanalysis depend on their analysts to maintain their analytic position through thick and thin…. Although analysands often seem to throw obstacles in the way of analysis, they do hope that their analysts will stand fast. (p. xi)

With this opening sentence, Roy Schafer introduces a subject that is as simple and complex as the title of this book: the all-too-common yet most difficult of clinical problems, namely the ‘bad feelings’ that arise for myriad reasons in our patients. David Black

David Black

30 Cholmley Gardens, London NW6 1AG. [email: dmblack@clara.co.uk]

David Black  

Consciousness was described by Freud as ‘a fact without parallel’. This paper suggests that the attempts by modern psychology and neuroscience to understand consciousness have failed to appreciate that it lies for clear and necessary reasons beyond the reach of ‘science’ as we have understood it since the seventeenth century. The author goes on to argue that the fact of consciousness implies a world of subjectivity and uniqueness which will only be integrated with the world of empirical science if there can be profound changes in our understanding of science itself; or, alternatively, if clear bounds are recognized to science's domain.

Rina Elieli  

When I was asked to write a review of Terrorism and War, I agreed at once. Later I began to wonder how I could have agreed to take on such a staggering task without a second thought, without first reading the book.

After I read and was greatly impressed by the book, I couldn't get myself to sit down and write a review although the book was so informative, so intriguing, so well written, and also to a great extent cast light on human phenomena that are very difficult to explain and understand. I learned a great deal from the book and, as I read it, I felt that my thoughts about a subject I had never been able to understand, and had always thought no mortal could understand, were becoming more and more well ordered. Nonetheless, I found that writing about this important, special book had become unbearably, almost impossibly difficult for me. I felt bad about it, since I had promised to write the review and even to meet a deadline. I didn't meet it. I felt as if I were being terrorized from the inside, from a commitment I had undertaken and couldn't fulfill.

But how could this be? After all, I'm a person, a woman, who has lived her whole life in wars and, in recent years, even more difficult, under terrorism, terrorism that dictates our way of life from morning to morning, without, perhaps, anyone of us being able to say to himself, that's how it is, our lives are dictated and controlled for many, many years by terror and war. And when I refer to ‘our lives’, I mean the inner as well as the outer. Inner life - yes, anxieties, imagination, thoughts, the inner space, breathing space, the ability to hope, to believe, to plan and to find myself saying each time that planning is a sign and promise of long life. And when I say long life, I don't mean only for myself and those close to me, but for all of us, for our country, our neighbours, for the whole world. (And always, just to be on the safe side, I mutter ‘this crazy world’.) How can anyone live with the whole world (‘this crazy world’) from morning to morning? And what about our private lives? What about privacy? I could see how life in the shadow of terrorism and war fosters magic thinking in a person's brain. And added to all this is the thought that anyone who lives under terrorism all of his life is supposed to get used to it! Isn't that how it is? But often, the terrorist inside him will grow and grow.
