Dear Editor

I write as a ‘parasite’ who has paid ‘£25 in order to bypass the … training of the British Psychoanalytical Society’, thereby ‘pass[ing] myself off to the public’ as a psychoanalyst (Carola Thorpe, Letters, BJP 20(3): 413-416). Carola Thorpe's letter cogently summarizes the position of the BPAS and, hence, of the British Confederation of Psychotherapists.

I would like to respond to the helpful comment made by the Editor in her introductory note to the publication of letters, including the one from Carola Thorpe. Ann Scott wrote that publication of the letters would enable the BJP readership to come to a ‘considered, well-informed view about whether The College is divisive, or is making a sincere attempt to achieve pluralism in a divided profession’.

Our profession has certainly suffered from divisiveness in recent years and, in the spirit of Ann Scott's words, I would draw your readers' attention to the following:

-the foundation of the BCP itself in 1993, which was triggered by the refusal of the 1992 United Kingdom Standing Conference on Psychotherapy (as it then was) AGM to accept a resolution proposed by the BPAS for what they termed a ‘Security Council’ model for the organization of the profession of psychotherapy. In this model, all serious power and responsibility were to reside in a small number of long established training bodies. Majority decisions of the ‘Security Council’ were to be absolutely binding on the whole organization. Had the ‘Security Council’ model been established, the effect would have been to dominate the whole field of psychotherapy, not only psychoanalysis. This resolution had been prepared for by meetings of a closed and self-selected sub-group of the then Psychoanalytic and Psychodynamic Psychotherapy Section of the UKSCP plus representatives of the British Psycho-Analytical Society (as it then was), which was in fact a member of another Section altogether. The existence of the sub-group was not secret but it had been assumed by the rest of the Section that it was discussing proposed developments within the Section, not the formation of a new body.

Warren Colman

Warren Colman

16 Chequer Street, St Albans, Herts AL1 3YD

Warren Colman  

Dear Editor

I feel reluctant to enter the debate about The College of Psychoanalysts because of the level of conflict and hostility any contribution is likely to generate from one quarter or another. Yet, in a way, this is just the point I want to make. Notwithstanding any other motives behind the setting up of The College of Psychoanalysts, it would be disingenuous of its founders to claim that they were surprised that it has had such a divisive impact. Its explicit intention is to mount an attack on the long-standing convention in this country, whereby, at least within the psychotherapy profession, the term ‘psychoanalyst’ is restricted to members of the Institute of Psychoanalysis. Outside the profession, of course, in a world in which psychotherapists are regularly called counsellors and many people do not understand the difference between a psychiatrist, a psychologist and a psychotherapist, our political disputes over nomenclature have all the hallmarks of a bunch of angels squabbling over who is entitled to a place on the head of the psychoanalytic pin.

I do have some sympathy for the Lacanians who find themselves in the anomalous position of being the only Lacanian analysts in Europe (or the rest of the world?) unable to call themselves psychoanalysts. I feel less sympathy for the psychoanalytic psychotherapists who wish to assume this title since their existing title, while unwieldy, has become standard usage over the past 20 years. If some psychoanalytic psychotherapists start calling themselves psychoanalysts while the majority do not, this can only add to the already existing confusion both inside and outside the profession.

I find many of Haya Oakley's arguments (BJP 20(4): 574-576) disingenuous in a similar way. She argues that if we want to stop psychoanalytic psychotherapy being restricted to psychologists and medics, we should all stand together behind the banner of psychoanalysis as the French have done. Yet given that the label of psychoanalyst is so contentious in this country, such a call to arms is contradictory: it sows dissension at the very point where we need unity.

Psychoanalytic Dialogues 13(6), 743-775, 2003

Introduction: A Systems View

Beatrice Beebe, Steven Knoblauch, Judith Rustin Amd Dorienne Sorter

Our goal in this series of four papers is a further refinement of a theory of interaction for psychoanalysis, with a specific focus on the concept of intersubjectivity. Psychoanalysis has addressed the concept of intersubjectivity primarily in the verbal/explicit mode. In contrast, infant research has addressed the concept of intersubjectivity in the nonverbal/implicit mode of action sequences, or procedural knowledge. We propose that an integration of explicit/linguistic with implicit/nonverbal theories of intersubjectivity is essential to a deeper understanding of therapeutic action in psychoanalysis today. To shed light on an implicit/nonverbal dimension of intersubjectivity in psychoanalysis, we include concepts from adult psychoanalysis, infant research, developmental systems theories, and nonverbal communication, particularly the distinction between implicit processing out of awareness and explicit processing at the declarative/verbal level. We conclude with an adult psychoanalytic case illustrating the integration of implicit/nonverbal forms of intersubjectivity into adult treatment.

Psychoanalytic Dialogues 14(1), 119-130, 2004

A Little Psyche-Music

Michael Eigen

A basic rhythm of breakdown-recovery, with many offshoots and permutations, characterizes aspects of psychic life. This rhythm threads its way through Elkin's, Winnicott's, and Bion's work and plays an important role in the unconscious processing of affects. If this rhythm is damaged or jammed, affect processing goes awry. Dream work helps initiate affect processing, a kind of emotional digestion. If the dream work's rhythm of breakdown-recovery is damaged, one lives in a state of chronic emotional indigestion or starvation. Clinical work, including a child's dream of the World Trade Center disaster, illustrates the discussion.

International Journal of Behavioral Development 28(1)

Editorial

Rachel Winter

Rachel Winter

[rachelwinterbjp@aol.com]

Rachel Winter  

Imagine how difficult it is to make a small selection from more than 400 papers, themselves originally picked out from countless numbers of articles submitted to the Journal over the last 20 years.

All the members of the editorial board were involved in the choosing of papers for this retrospective issue to mark the 20th anniversary of the BJP. The consultant editors were also asked to make suggestions. Between us we read through all the papers and then began a long process of selecting and discarding, arguing and compromising, to produce a long list, a shorter list, a shortlist, a revised shortlist, another revised shortlist and, finally, a contents list. This was a huge amount of work but I am very pleased to say that after all that, everyone concerned has at least one paper that they picked, in this issue.

Of course I did worry that we would end up with something that resembled a horse designed by committee. And perhaps we have. But it seemed important to me that we all had a hand in this, because the editorial board of the BJP, uniquely, is made up of representatives from nine psychotherapy organizations, some BCP, some UKCP, and these nine people from nine different trainings work together to produce this Journal.

Edward Said described the West-Eastern Divan Orchestra that he founded with Daniel Barenboim thus, ‘It doesn't pretend to be building bridges and all that hokey stuff. But there it is, a paradigm of coherent and intelligent living together’. The politics of our little profession are nothing in comparison to those bitter and bloody divisions, yet I like to think that, in its very small way, the BJP also might provide a sort of clearing amongst the trees in which something productive and creative can happen.

As a child I used to go with my grandmother to auctions where she bought trunks of antique clothes and textiles. The pleasure of delving into these never paled, never disappointed. You might find anything; a pink ostrich-feather cape, frail lace, crêpe de Chine, rose-red taffeta, pale jade shantung, tortoiseshell combs, cloisonné buckles, beadwork, violet and tarnished silver ribbons, wilted felt flowers.

Postscript: ‘I Was so Much Older Then …’

Jeremy Holmes

Jeremy Holmes

Jeremy Holmes  

If I were sent this article to review by the BJP today I suspect I would sit on the fence about whether or not to recommend publication. Following conventional etiquette I would start by finding a few things about it to praise: quite interesting in a slightly off-beat way, good discussion of the poem, not badly written although occasionally somewhat pompous especially in the opening page, clinical examples competently handled (but has he got written permission to publish these details?).

Then I would start to pull it apart. What exactly is the author trying to say and where precisely is he (assuming it is a he as BJP articles are, of course, anonymized) coming from? Is he a middle-grouper, a Jungian, an interpersonalist, or what? Why all this emphasis on Rycroft, a somewhat marginal figure? Why not talk about psychotherapeutic process in its own terms, without having to muddy the waters by bringing in poetry for goodness' sake - most people hate or ignore the stuff anyway? And all this psychotherapy/neurology stuff at the end seems rather out of date - hasn't he heard of Solms (1997), Schore (2003), Gerhardt (2004) et al.?

Well, what was I trying to say, and where was I coming from? At one level the latter is fairly straightforward: I was (literally) coming from therapy with Charles Rycroft, and wanting to fly the Rycroftian flag (see Pearson 2004) - my post-therapy positive transference/idealization at that stage still somewhat unresolved. At another, I was simply following my own personal form of eclecticism and wanting to see if one could think about psychotherapy in the same sort of terms as poetry. The question remains - why should one have wanted to do that?

I suppose my answer would be that the paper was an early attempt to tackle a problem which I continue to see as largely unresolved: the huge discrepancy between psychoanalytic theory and what actually goes on in the consulting room between patient and therapist. And, in a Rycroftian way, I think there is an inherent difficulty for psychoanalytic theory in theorizing itself. Turning to a discipline outside psychotherapy for illumination was an attempt to overcome this problem.

Warren Colman

Warren Colman

16 Chequer Street, St Albans, Herts AL1 3YD. [email: wgc.net2mail@ntlworld.com]

Warren Colman  

This paper was written after, but published prior to ‘Aspects of anima and animus in oedipal development’ (Colman 1996) in which I set out to ‘rehabilitate anima and animus for clinical use’. Both these papers represented my personal attempt to integrate Jungian and psychoanalytic thinking in the distinctive tradition of the Society of Analytical Psychology.

Jung's ideas about anima and animus had first inspired my interest in Jungian psychology so I had been disappointed and perplexed when I could not find a way to integrate these ideas with the predominantly object relations perspective of my clinical training. It was through working with couples that I eventually began to recognize Jung's typical ‘pen pictures’ of anima and animus possession and to notice (a) that such people tended to be married to each other and (b) that their difficulties could also be expressed in terms of oedipal development. However, like most of Jung's major concepts, anima and animus are multi-faceted and this way of seeing them as oedipally derived internal objects underplayed their meaning as psychic functions operating as ‘a bridge to the unconscious’ (Jung 1928, para. 339). A subsequent paper, ‘Contrasexuality and the unknown soul’ (Colman 1998) attempted to redress this balance.

Although the clinical material in the ‘cross-gender’ paper is drawn from couple psychotherapy, I had not seen it as primarily about couples but rather as a paper about gender identity. I was sorry that the BJP had published it under the heading ‘couples’ as I thought this obscured its primary intention. This may have been partly due to the relative unfamiliarity and specificity of the couple focus. While the contribution of child psychotherapy to psychoanalytic theory has long been recognized, couple psychotherapy still seems to be seen as merely an ‘application’ of psychoanalysis and its distinctive contribution to the field as a whole is rarely recognized.

WARREN COLMAN is a Professional Member of the Society of Analytical Psychology and a Full Member of the Society of Couple Psychoanalytic Psychotherapists. Formerly a senior staff member at the Tavistock Marital Studies Institute, he is now in full-time private practice in St Albans. A Brief Personal Memoir of Wilfred Bion

First published in BJP 9(1), 1992

John Hill

John Hill

27 Martingale Close, Ham Common, Richmond TW10 7JJ

John Hill  

I first met Bion in 1949, knew him socially for some years and then, in the course of analytic training, went to him for supervision of my second case some nine years later and continued this for several years after qualification. In the course of supervision, as in some of his writing, he tended to emphasize the importance of not making undue efforts to remember specific ideas, but would say instead: ‘Let the patient remind you’. I have found this comment pertinent to his own ideas and, in over 30 years of analysing, supervising and teaching, I have found myself both with patients and perhaps particularly with students reminded more often of things that Bion has said than any other single source of my inspiration. It is because I have found myself in this way so often reminded of Bion that I have been moved to write this short paper, not with any idea of a systematic evaluation, but rather anecdotally to describe some of his perceptions that have come most frequently to my own mind in the course of both treating patients and teaching students.

My experience was that Bion's technique as a supervisor differed sharply from others; in particular, from those supervisors who combined an insistence that their students should not take notes during sessions with a requirement that in supervision they should attempt rigorously to reproduce the minute by minute, word by word detail of the session. Whether this is still widely practised I do not know but even then it seemed to me that such a requirement was perhaps impossible to the point of absurdity. In contrast Bion would sometimes say: ‘Don't take notes, keep a diary and on those days when you curse the day you ever heard of psychoanalysis put that down in your diary’. He reminds me of a lecturer in philosophy at Oxford (Gilbert Ryle) who would tell his students that if he caught anyone taking notes in his lectures he would send them out for inattention.

I was never quite able to put his advice about the diary into practice but here I must put my association with Bion into a broader personal context.

Meg Williams

Meg Williams

Meg Williams  

Don's parents were Jewish émigrés from Latvia whom he described as ‘the miracle in his life’. His father, a builder and businessman, whom he admired intensely, did not force him in any particular direction but encouraged his emerging interests - such as, in the early days, riding lessons in Central Park. A photograph shows Don as a child mounted on an Arab stallion, in company with his father - who is riding a donkey.

As a child he was not studious. Like Keats, he never read a book until his early teens, but instead established himself amongst his peers as a fighter. As a result of his physique, name and bellicose propensities, he became known at school as ‘Tubby Belcher’. This early pattern found a repetition when, around the middle of his career, he quarrelled with the British Psychoanalytic Institute and eventually got himself ejected. The subject of the dispute was in fact dear to his heart, and a matter on which he could not compromise: it concerned his firm belief that ‘education’ must be distinguished from ‘training’.

In his middle years, after having married into our very literary family, he became increasingly fond of reading - ‘addicted’ as he said. Poetry was a brave new world that opened to him at that time and led to the establishment of the Clunie Press (started by Don and my mother, Martha Harris, in memory of my father, a poet and teacher). His lifelong passion for art and architecture, however, dated back to the time when his parents took him, aged 8, on a six-month tour of Europe. This led ultimately to his core philosophy of the ‘aesthetic conflict’, as formulated in The Apprehension of Beauty.

In childhood, he said, he had been fascinated by the country that produced Winnie the Pooh. Then, as a medical student at Yale, he stumbled across the writings of Melanie Klein. His desire to come to England became overwhelming and he wangled the terms of his military service to get himself deposited on the couch in her consulting-room. His analysis, which he began in 1954, he described in terms of a breathless and dangerous ride - ‘but wonderful’. He knew she knew he was not simply a nice, sporty American boy. But he was not an uncritical Anglophile. Anti-Semitism and xenophobia enraged him, and he saw these as endemic in the British establishment.

Psychoanalytic Inquiry24(2), 286-308, 2004

History of a Childhood Neurosis and its Relation to the Adult Superego

R. Curtis Bristol

The purpose of this paper is to find meaning for the ‘presence of conscience’ observable in the psychoanalytic setting and corresponding evidence for the origins of such ways of thinking, feeling, and remembering. I apply this perspective to the case study of a man who presented as constricted, inhibited, anxious and self-critical. He was outwardly successful but internally tormented with what can best be described as an obsessional neurosis. His initial symptomatic neurosis was supplanted by a transference neurosis reflecting a childhood obsessional neurosis. In my theory of mind during this analysis, I often saw the original ideas of Freud at work - unconscious sense of guilt, ego ideal and conscience. The analysand represented over and over the dynamics of the Oedipus stage of development. I made additional observations about character formation and guilt. The analysand terminated his work with me symptom-free. From this case study, I learned that the presence of conscience (guilt and self-denigration), or of superego structure and function in classical terms, is best approached as to origin by following the development of self in reference to the other.



Psychoanalytic Dialogues14(3), 289-311, 2004

Impasse Recollected in Tranquillity: Love, Dissociation and Discipline in the Analytic Process

Stuart A. Pizer

This paper offers an intimate account of a long-term analytic process and a detailed presentation of one pivotal session to illustrate and explore the issues of love, dissociation and discipline in a therapeutic relationship. Organized around the concept of impasse, this paper presents a relational perspective on the potential in transference and countertransference love to facilitate or curtail the forward progress of therapeutic work. Love may bring life or impasse to a person in analysis. One key to the dynamics of therapeutic love and impasse is the problem of weak dissociation (Stern 1997) and the impact of the analyst's noticing, or not noticing, a moment in the onrush of familiar clinical process that is ripe for questioning. A new concept is introduced and elaborated in this paper that relates to the resolution of preoedipal and oedipal transference love: the paradoxical analytic triangle.

In this paper I have sought to shift the focus on the construction of memory within psychotherapeutic practice in a number of different directions to draw some more general lessons for the process and status of therapeutic accounts. The precipitating context for the current scrutiny of memory-making within therapy may have limited its scope and fruitfulness. The fact that this issue was largely prompted by debates about the status of (usually) adult women's recovery of memories of early abuse within therapy is a relevant factor that has been compounded by issues of professional credibility and hierarchy. Clearly, at a cultural level, women's memories of childhood abuse function politically as well as personally, as reflected by the social and legal responses to this challenge.

However, guidelines for professional practice cannot legislate for the indeterminacies surrounding the subjectivity of memory, while assumptions underlying the empirical psychological resources drawn upon to inform debates in psychotherapy require critical scrutiny. Clinical and interpretive dilemmas extend beyond the status accorded client memorial reports to therapists' memory-making practices as textualized via both supervision and clinical note-taking. Drawing on more recent (including feminist) discussions of memory that identify different political possibilities within third and first person accounts it was suggested that, rather than eschewing the subjectivity of memory, therapists can instead analyse this as a key interpretive and reflexive resource to inform their own practice.

Paul Williams

15 Arden Road, London N3 3AB. [email: p.williams@apu.ac.uk]

Paul Williams  

I would like to comment, perhaps a little more discursively than the other papers you will hear today, on some of the problems posed by free association for many contemporary analytic patients.

Free associations are never free, or at least when they are relatively free this is a sign of successful therapy or a mature character. The freedom to associate does not imply an absence of determination, but the elimination of the voluntary selection of thoughts and a reduction in censorship between consciousness and the preconscious. In this way unconscious defences are revealed.

For psychotherapists and analysts to discuss together free association is very important, in my view. Free association is a subject that precedes theory, and can therefore provide us all with common conceptual ground. Free association is not divorced from theory, but it is a method and a process derived from clinical observation, rather than theory. Only with the selection procedure - that is, the choosing of which elements of free association to emphasize or otherwise - do the theoretical differences between clinicians become apparent. What unites our pluralistic, divided discipline is a commitment to the free association method and its meaning.

Freud employed the metaphor of a train to describe free association, inviting patients to reflect on their own thoughts as if they were in a train observing them as they went on their way. What is revealed by this process is a train of thought, sometimes clear, more often than not obscure, usually requiring time to elicit and occasionally destined to remain elusive. By placing the patient in the unusual position of observer of his or her own thoughts, with the aim of facilitating associations between what is present and what is absent, Freud created an unusual form of personal anthropology. We become the ethnographer and indigenous object of study at the same time. There is an unconscious other to whom we relate.

Into the Woods: Beyond the Frame

Marilyn Mathew

Marilyn Mathew

London

Marilyn Mathew  

Art that touches the soul is rare and numinous, opening some kind of portal in the mind that transports us to another dimension. Paintings that speak volumes often defy verbal description but, like dreams, these magical visual experiences can stay with us all our lives, tugging persistently at our curiosity, insisting on reflection and reconnection with the initial wonder. The more I gaze at, absorb and analyse a captivating image, the more I see in it and understand about it - the more I realize there is to be seen. The more I wonder about its numinous effect, the more I discover about myself personally, culturally, collectively and spiritually.

Recently, on the basis of a small colour reproduction in the Tate Magazine, I went to the Alan Cristea Gallery in London's Cork Street to see a new collection of work by Howard Hodgkin. ‘Into the Woods’ is a series of four large abstract prints, one for each season. I have always loved Hodgkin's work - he is an exhilarating colourist - but I was not prepared for the impact that hit me when I walked through the door and saw ‘Spring’.

Hot on the heels of amazement, reeling from the impact of the vibrant colour and trying to catch my breath, I began to think: ‘Why - what is it that is so special about this image? Why do I want to bask in front of it endlessly? Did the artist hope or mean to touch me so profoundly? He seems to have captured a moment … is it about spring or a symbolic personal experience? Do we share a moment in time or does this represent something out of time? Is it simply my own meaning which I invest in transference or is there something more collective and archetypal going on here?’

The print is enormous: 2 × 3 metres, a two-part hand-painted lift-ground etching with coarse aquatint and carborundum etching. Swirling with turquoise and vibrant blues, there is a single large arching shape in greens the colour of new beech leaves. Its size is impressive, the colours - typical of Hodgkin - are clear and pure, the brush stokes exuberant. The whole effect is, to me, thoroughly uplifting. Why?

Plundering the Dead: Anatomy Artist, Gunther von Hagens, Exhibits his ‘Plastinates’ (Berlin, February-September 2001)

Tessa Adams

Tessa Adams

London

Tessa Adams  

Perhaps one of the most direct questions that provokes an unequivocal response is, ‘What do you want to happen to your body after you are dead?’ As we know, the main options in the Western economy are burial or

551

cremation, and the answer ‘I don't know’ or ‘I don't mind’ would be the least typical. In fact, more usually something like ‘I couldn't bear to be put in the ground to rot’ or ‘I couldn't bear to be burnt’ would be the reply. Furthermore, people imply that they know what is at stake by debating the various benefits of their choice. Notwithstanding those individuals who bid for what can be seen to be a socially responsible option, like offering their organs to medical science, the decision about what happens to our bodies after death is largely subjective. Yet one thing that we seem fairly certain about is that, whichever option we might choose, it would be expected that, after the funeral, our body would not become a subject for the public gaze. For relinquishing our corporeality to others for disposal is both veiled in ceremony and constituted as sacred. Thus coffins are designed to shroud, curtains to conceal, and autopsies are medically regulated, serving the prevailing belief that, whatever happens, the dead are to rest in peace. Therefore it is not surprising that, when hoarded body parts of children were recently discovered in a British hospital vault, controversy was bound to follow.

It is within this context that I will ask you to consider the issues that are raised by the extraordinary work of the Anatomy Artist, Gunther von Hagens. For this is a man who trades the dead as his product utilizing the actual cadaver to serve his aesthetic enterprise. Situated as both sculpture and science his exhibits immortalize the dead to stand naked before us, stripped of skin, prised apart with muscles gleaming, their flesh is transposed to banish the vestiges of suffering in an enduring plastic counterpart. So distinct is the protest surrounding Hagens's work that not only has he been challenged as an anatomist by the medical profession and the Church, but several European galleries fear the prospect of outrage should they exhibit him.

Editorial

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

[annscottbjp@aol.com]

Ann Scott  

Working with severely disturbed patients, as Marguerite Valentine writes in this issue, is one of the most challenging and difficult areas of practice. If suicide is a risk, or takes place, immense anxiety is generated, in individuals and in systems. The three papers which begin this issue tackle this individual and systemic anxiety dispassionately and movingly. They also probe the ethical and management dilemmas which suicide poses. Rose Hamilton, meditating on a suicide that took place a year ago, asks whether it is possible to contain very damaged patients without medication, in a therapeutic milieu. She considers the impact of a suicide on herself as a worker in a residential setting, questioning her ‘idealized image, of both the institution and client group’. Hamilton, publishing under a pseudonym because of the delicacy of the situation, notes that working with suicidal clients in a therapeutic milieu ‘often led to creativity in the work, and a more profound level of connection with the residents; this made the act, I believe, even more penetrating’. Next, Marguerite Valentine, describing the suicide of a male patient in her private practice with a five-year psychiatric history, explores the ‘maddening’ experience of the work, and tracks her evolving countertransference responses to her patient. She explores the ambience of the sessions, her developing realization of the patient's involvement with the psychiatric system, and her thoughts about what may have been in his mind when he took his life. With Gertrud Mander's paper we move from the direct impact of the interpersonal encounter into something more modulated - the encounter with a text, and with a more optimistic view of suicide: David Malan's view of the suicidal impulse as a treatable condition, and reversible when the therapist allies himself with the ‘Cord of Life’, which Malan sees as most active when a suicide attempt fails. Nevertheless, Mander poses difficult questions, such as can the follow-up and patients' letters over many years validate his theory of the Cord of Life?

Psychoanalysis and Racism: Some Further Thoughts

Paul Gordon

Paul Gordon

Paul Gordon  

Events of the last 10 years or so since my original article was published can leave no doubt of the continuing power of racism, of the terrible consequences of treating people not just as different but as other to ourselves and less than human. They leave no doubt either as to how easy it seems to be for ordinary people, given the ‘right’ context, to slip into being not just bystanders to evil but active participants in it.

There is, I think, a certain naivety at work in my original article, a belief that psychoanalysis might help us to address this terrible problem. Since writing it I have moved a long way from such a position. Having started out trying to use psychoanalytic ideas to think about social and political matters, I have come to accept a division between the world of the consulting room and clinical practice and the political and social world. Whatever insights psychoanalysis might have, whatever validity its theories may hold, these are not to be applied to the world at large but are limited in application to the clinical encounter and to the immediate context of the individual.

Freud, it is often remarked, could be somewhat disdainful of clinical work, and his attempts to make a larger mark on the world through general theories of culture and society are understandable. But this does not mean we have to accept them as true. Freud's work moreover, it should be added, is often tainted with its own racism, something I had not addressed in this paper.

Not in Our Name

Bernardine Bishop , Rachael Davenhill and Julia Vellacott

Julia Vellacott

London

Julia Vellacott  

Dear Editor

In February 2003, shortly before the invasion of Iraq, a number of us felt that it was important to protest as a professional group against the impending war. We prepared at very short notice a letter for the press to be sent to all BCP members with an available email address. (We were enormously indebted to Bill Chambers for the technical work of this.) The statement read as follows:

We, the undersigned individuals working as psychotherapists and psychoanalysts, wish to express our profound opposition to the attack on Iraq currently being prepared by our government and by the United States. We wish to make clear that these actions are not in our name.

A total of 177 individuals responded and asked for their names to be put to the letter. The statement and names were then sent to ten national and London newspapers, and the statement published in The Independent on Sunday on 19 February 2003. The paper used one name (from the top of the alphabet) for each organization represented. We emailed to each signatory a copy of the statement and the list of names to use for further individual work such as writing to their local MP or newspaper.

We felt, given the time-frame we were working to, that the response was heartening, and are aware from subsequent discussions that many other people would have added their name had there been time to write to them. As people will be aware, there have been a number of other contributions from the world of psychotherapy and psychoanalysis, including books, lectures and workshops. We hope that we can continue to engage as professionals in public debate on these issues.

Yours sincerely

Bernardine Bishop

Freud and the Non-European by Edward Said. Published by Verso, London, 2003; 84 pp; £11.50.

Marco Chiesa

Marco Chiesa

Consultant Psychiatrist in Psychotherapy
The Cassel Hospital, Richmond TW10 7JF
[m.chiesa@ucl.ac.uk]

Marco Chiesa  

This book reproduces the lecture that the late Edward Said, Professor of English and Comparative Literature at Columbia University, delivered at the Freud Museum of London in 2001. Said's qualifications on the subject are rooted in a combination of painful life experiences and academic excellence. As Dr Christopher Bollas remarks in his excellent and informative introduction, Said and his family were driven from their home in Palestine after the 1948 war. Said went into exile in the USA where he was educated and subsequently became one of the most respected thinkers in his field. He was always involved in politics and was a member of the Palestinian National Council between 1977 and 1991. In his political writings Said made use of psychoanalytical concepts to understand the events in the Middle East. For example, as Bollas reminds us, Said thoroughly examined the structure of Israeli oppression of the Palestinians during the 35 years of occupation of the West Bank and Gaza following the 1967 war. Projection of violence by successive Israeli governments as well as the psychology of the stubborn refusal to recognize both Palestinian national identity and Palestinians as people deserving of the same basic human rights as accorded to Israelis, are amongst Said's themes elaborated in one of his most well-known books, The Question of Palestine(1979).

The term ‘Non-European’ used by Said in this book is to be understood within the framework of nineteenth and twentieth-century European history, which was characterized by often brutal and violent colonial occupation of land and the subjugation of entire populations throughout the world. The resulting dominant ideology, predominantly Eurocentric, tended to be dismissive of other cultures as intrinsically inferior. As a psychiatrist I was intrigued to learn in Freud and the Non-European of the scientific view held by a Professor Porot who diagnosed indigenous Algerians as possessing ‘… no cortex; or, more precisely, [the Algerian] is dominated, like the inferior vertebrates, by the diencephalons. The cortical functions, if they exist at all, are very feeble, and are practically unintegrated into the dynamic of existence’ (p. 19, citing Fanon, The Wretched of the Earth). Profesor Porot is in line with other distinguished European clinical psychiatrists who labelled the native as a savage killer who kills for no reason. In my view, it is also thanks to the application of this type of science to the practice of colonial conquest that the mass murder of hundreds of thousands of the indigenous population, regarded as intrinsically an inferior race, could be executed without eliciting horror and shock in the societies in whose names these acts were carried out.

Patients Who are Not Ready for Interpretations

First published in BJP 7(1), 1990

Josephine Klein

Josephine Klein

58 Roupell Street, London SE 1 8TB

Josephine Klein  

‘Patients who are not ready for interpretations’. A friend criticized this title on the ground that it implies some unreadiness on the part of the patient, not to be ready for something. As though patients ought to be available for interpretations, as though interpretation is what psychotherapy is about. This is not what I believe. Psychotherapy is therapy: it is about enabling people to explore their processes, conscious and unconscious, so that they can understand better what they are doing in their lives and gain some control over the alternatives which are in principle available to them. We know that it can be helpful, in pursuit of this goal, to interpret to people the unconscious meaning of what they are doing or feeling or thinking. But we also know of people we are not able to help by this means, and therefore a more accurate if clumsier title would have been ‘Patients for whom interpretations are inappropriate’. Or, even more accurately, ‘Patients for whom interpretation of unconscious material is inappropriate’. What I find inappropriate with particular people is for me to bring in aspects of their experience of which they are unconscious, which are ego-alien to them and sound strange to them.

My first example is of someone who could not tolerate what she experienced as my intrusiveness.

I saw ‘Rose’ for more than 10 years, from her early twenties onwards. She came twice a week to me individually and once a week to a group I run. She was dreadfully depressed, anxious, and generally unalive, living most of the time in what she described as a grey fog. In the first couple of years I interpreted in the normal way what I thought was happening to her or between us. She seemed to listen to what I said, often agreeing, and we got nowhere much except that she did keep coming.

This book is an exhaustive survey of the literature of transsexualism. Colette Chiland is Psychiatrist-in-Chief at the Alfred-Binet Centre and Professor Emeritus of Clinical Psychology at René Descartes University in Paris. She is the author of several books, including Homo Psychanalyticus (1990).

Transsexualism is the state of mind which knows itself to be the sex other than the anatomical sex to which the person is born. It is not a wish to become a person of the other sex but literally the knowledge that one is already. This is different from transvestism, a desire and compulsion to assume the clothing of the opposite sex which, for men, includes sexual pleasure.

1. A Brief Re-Acquaintance with Jung's Analytic Technique

Ann Kutek

Ann Kutek

32 Lillie Road, London SW6 1TN

Ann Kutek  

For some years now, I have been offering a time-limited psychotherapy to particular patients in the context of a private analytic practice. I shall give here a clinical vignette of an intervention with someone who, though domiciled in the UK, worked abroad and returned for a monthly stay two or three times a year. We were able to meet for two sets of five sessions. Having learned the precipitating reason for the referral, I agreed to set up a first session.

He arrived fractionally ahead of time. I led him straight into the consulting room. He struck me as someone who could readily disappear in a crowd, dressed in dark casual clothes, hunched into himself as if stiffened by arthritis, not tall, and fashionably unshaven. I directed him to one of the chairs and he perched on it. I asked him what he wished to work on. He told me he had asked to be referred following successful cancer treatment one year earlier and having just been medically confirmed as symptom-free. Despite all assurances, he still felt uneasy. He had been treated by ‘the best man in the country’ for his complaint who had given him the all clear and yet the part of the sentence that constantly rang in his ears was: ‘But, of course, there could always be the one rogue cell’. The thought invaded all his waking hours and the only way he had of controlling it was to work obsessively, but he feared he might eventually drop from exhaustion.

Observing my initial response, I had the feeling he had brought his disabling fear to me and that I, knowing how briefly he would be in the UK, felt acutely pressured to decide whether I had anything to offer in a time-limited modality or was the whole enterprise doomed. He may have picked up my hesitation and told me that 20 years ago he had had four times a week psychoanalysis over three years with Dr S, of whom I had heard but did not know personally. He felt that thanks to him he was able to progress in his career.

To Redeem One Person is to Redeem the World: The Life of Frieda Fromm-Reichmann by Gail Hornstein (New York: Free Press, 2000; 478 pages)Female Genius: Life, Madness, Words - Hannah Arendt, Melanie Klein, Colette, Volumes 1 and 2 by Julie Kristeva (New York: Columbia University Press, 2001; 291 and 296 pages)

Janet Sayers

Janet Sayers

University of Kent British Association of Psychotherapists

Janet Sayers  

The attunement or empathy of psychotherapists with their patients in enabling them to become more fully conscious of what is going on in and around them (rather than suffer the ills of unconsciousness) is often equated with femininity. Specifically it is equated with women's empathy in looking after and mothering others. But what is empathy? These books, by and about women, provide two rather different answers, as I will seek to illustrate and explain. Gail Hornstein's very readable biography of Frieda Fromm-Reichmann highlights the immediate, other-directed empathy or intuition of another's feelings from their facial and other bodily expressions. Julia Kristeva's much less easily readable account of Klein's work highlights the self-generated empathy involved in projecting or imagining oneself, as it were, into the shoes of another.

I will begin with Hornstein's book To Redeem One Person is to Redeem the World: The Life of Frieda Fromm-Reichmann. Hornstein is a women's studies psychologist. She situates empathy as intuition in the context of Frieda Fromm-Reichmann's achievement in helping pioneer the psychoanalytically-based therapeutic community treatment of schizophrenics in Germany and America. In recounting her life, Hornstein makes much of the teaching of the Jewish religion in which Frieda was brought up regarding putting others first so as to redeem and enable their spirit to flourish. To this Hornstein adds other details of Frieda's early life. She recounts her birth in Karlsruhe on 23 October 1889, followed by the birth of two younger sisters, Grete and Anna. She also recounts examples of Frieda's very early intuition of the feelings of others in her immediate childhood home, and later of psychiatric patients from her first days in medical school, which she began in 1908. Hornstein also recounts Frieda's work as foster-mother to the child of one of her friends, and her self-sacrificing feeling for others in treating non-paying as well as fee-paying patients in a private clinic in Dresden, and in subsequently establishing in 1924 a therapeutic community in Heidelberg.

Harold Bourne

Harold Bourne

Rome

Harold Bourne  

Dear Editor

My first reply to James Taylor and Alec McGuire's letters about ‘A homosexual turns to women’ wasn't solemn and serious. This one is.

First, let us remember the death while seeking immortality of Maui, the hero of Maori legend, who fished out of the ocean the Land of the Long White Cloud, today's New Zealand. He was to achieve eternal life by creeping into the vagina, up through the womb, and out of the mouth of his ancestress, Hine-Nui-Te-Po, Daughter of the Night. She had a body like a man's and a mouth and vagina lined with teeth like a barracuda's, but as hard as volcanic glass. Unluckily, when he was up to his waist inside her, while all onlookers kept silent, a little fantail bird could hold back its laughter no longer. The old chieftainess awoke, closed her dreadful vagina on him, crushed him in its teeth, and Maui perished.

Second, a psychotherapy patient in whose world women were more than ordinarily fearsome, much attracted to the girl next door, but alarmed by her overtly seductive moves, produced Hine-Nui-Te-Po's ghost in a nightmare. His hand was terrifyingly trapped fast in the mouth of the nasty old mother of the girl next door, and he couldn't get it out. The inside of her mouth felt spiky all over like a cat's, and her tongue was rough and barbed.

The present letter is in response now to the latest correspondence which included a judiciously even-handed contribution from the Editor herself.

Anybody who isn't overheated about homosexuality, reading my paper calmly, would see that it is not about homosexuality as such. It is a case report about a young man seeking to shift from homo- to hetero-sexuality, and in anguish and confusion over the female genitalia. The remarkable and rare feature that prompted publishing it was his fascinating though tortured expression of phantasies about women that operate silently, undetected, but powerfully throughout humanity's affairs.

In the second sentence of my paper, I made it explicit that my patient's case could illuminate the normal developmental struggle that men have to achieve heterosexuality, and not just that achievement by this one homosexual patient. Mistakenly, I assumed that the Journal's readership needed no reminding of the universal phantasies about women that afflicted my patient and which, as I started this letter by illustrating, inspire humankind from old Maori legend to today's dreamer on the couch.

2. Obsession Transformed into Mourning

Gertrud Mander

Gertrud Mander

24 Chalcot Crescent, London NW1 8YD

Gertrud Mander  

The client was a handsome professional man, somewhat beyond midlife, with an easy rapport indicating a public-school upbringing. His father was a diplomat and in his early years the family moved around the world until they settled in England when he was seven. Boarding school compounded the instability of his life as did his parents' unstable marriage. In adolescence he had a persistent fantasy of marriage. He had his first serious relationship as a student, married three times and had three by now grown-up children. In his last marriage to a much younger woman he had felt special as never before, but that marriage also broke up six years ago, when he became deeply depressed. Medication helped him overcome this incapacitating condition, but life had become meaningless. He retired from work and became obsessed by fantasies of getting his third wife back which prevented him from picking up the pieces of his life constructively. Finally he asked for help on the advice of a former client of mine.

The Session

J came on time on a motorbike and sat down on the couch facing me. I opened the session by asking what he had come for to which he replied laconically: ‘I will tell you my life story’, whereupon he launched into a fluent and detailed chronological narrative, tracing the ups and downs of his marriages and of his more recent troubled singleness. I listened for 40 minutes, occasionally asking for clarification of a point, while trying to establish the presenting symptom and to find a pattern in this life story that might enable me to formulate a dynamic focus. Linking in my mind the instability of his early life with the ups and downs of his marriages, I also linked the adolescent fantasy of getting married with the precipitate remarriages and with the ongoing obsession about his last wife. I identified the obsession that he might get her back as a ‘psychic retreat’ (Steiner 1993).

Lindie White

Lindie White  

The appearance of this book coincides with a more general and explicit engagement of the psychoanalytic field with religion and spirituality and is not, I think, disconnected. For myself, I hope this indicates a coming

387

together of the poles that seemed to fly apart with Freud and Jung's split nearly a century ago, both of whom ‘lend’ their epigraphs to this book. In bringing together this anthology of essays by contributors of varying orientation, Nick Totton is arguing for an openness with regard to paranormal events by psychoanalytic practitioners. It has been something of a tradition, he writes, begun by Freud, for workers in this field to conceal their own opinions or to ‘express high-minded agnosticism’ (p. 12) despite, often, personal experience and/or a fascination with the subject. He and other contributors have had ‘experience enough to render the question of belief superfluous’ (p. 12). Taking Freud's familiar quote about the ‘apparent fact that the mental processes of one person … can be transferred to another person through empty space without employing the familiar methods of communication by means of words and signs’, Totton says this transference is variously called countertransference, projective identification or unconscious communication, all as if they answered the question of what is going on here.

Montague Ullman, an American psychoanalyst, became interested in telepathy by close encounters with the paranormal in his life and work. This led him to devote his time to experiment in order to gain scientific validity and his chapter explores some of his experiments in dream and telepathy. He concludes significantly that there are gains to be had from explicit recognition of the telepathy hypothesis, around disclosure and ‘a fairminded openness towards patients about the reality of telepathy rather than a denial or bias that confirms their fear of self-disclosure’ (p. 44). This is especially important as telepathic experience often occurs at critical moments in therapy as a last desperate effort at relatedness. It can be enlisted by the need for survival and development, a point also made by the Dutch psychoanalyst M. Lietaert Peerbolte.

Educational therapy is a specialized intervention which makes use of psychoanalytic insights to help children unravel their deep-seated reasons for not learning. Treatment normally takes place over four terms or more. When asked to see Jackson for a meagre seven sessions, for reasons of economics, I was sceptical that there would be any major shift in his view of himself and consequently in his behaviour.

Vignette: Jackson

He arrived ten minutes early and, when I went into the waiting room, he was snuggled up to his mother, leaning over her shoulder, looking at Cosmopolitan magazine. He glanced at me when I said ‘hello’ and then turned back. His mother got up and said, ‘Off you go. Be good for Mrs Beaumont. I'll see you later.’ And she hurriedly left the building.

Jackson walked ahead of me up the stairs, with a heavy tread and his feet turned outwards. As he entered, he gave the sand-pit a cursory glance and sat down. He turned to look at me, giving a half-smile, and then turned away. I said, ‘How's things?’

‘Fine’, he replied and looked at his drawing book, flicking the pages open and fiddling with the pens.

‘I've a feeling that you might like to draw a picture?’

Jackson gave a nod but sat with his hands still.

‘Maybe you would like to do a squiggle again?’

Again he nodded and produced two colours, giving me the blue. I closed my eyes and drew a blue line. He looked at it for a moment and decided instantly what to draw.

‘It's a bear,’ he said. ‘But this line is long because it went down here.’

‘Because I'd made a long line?’

‘Yes. It's only got a little tail.

Celia Downes

Celia Downes

Forum for Independent Psychotherapists, London

Celia Downes  

Although this is ostensibly a book about counselling elderly people, there is much here for psychotherapists working with people aged 60-90 plus in a range of settings. It would be useful for therapists working in a GP practice, in institutional settings such as a nursing homes or hospitals, or offering once-weekly work to older patients within the context of their private practice.

The author is an analytical psychotherapist who has written books on psychotherapy with older people and on attitudes to death and dying. This book draws on her experience of setting up a counselling service for older people in her local area. It explores what it is like to be old and how we can creatively be of help to people who have lived longer than ourselves. The reader is alerted to the hazards, obstacles and challenges involved in engaging with elderly people for whom the idea of counselling or psychotherapy is unfamiliar and possibly alien. Each chapter concludes with questions for reflection and discussion, making it a useful handbook for anyone interested in setting up similar local counselling services for older people, for those offering specialist training for counsellors and psychotherapists for such work and for their supervisors.

As an experienced tutor on a counselling course with an integrative theoretical perspective Orbach offers what she describes as an ‘easy eclecticism’. Her own approach is firmly underpinned by the discipline of her primarily Jungian psychodynamic framework, but she also includes and illustrates approaches which draw on object relations theory, attachment theory, humanistic approaches and some cognitive-behavioural techniques. Inevitably, in a slim volume, theory is touched upon rather than expounded, making this a suitable book for therapists already theoretically well grounded; beginners would need to acquire more detailed theoretical grounding alongside the specialist focus offered here. Orbach's concern is that workers should draw creatively and flexibly on their own theoretical framework, that they should be aware of the prejudice that most of us absorb in an ageist society and that they should think through the sort of adaptations they might need to make in particular circumstances. Her lively clinical vignettes aim to set the reader thinking and questioning; for example, how might she engage with an anxious elderly man who has just received a diagnosis of prostate cancer and arrives holding a newly lit cigarette? How does one work with a client in a nursing home subject to frequent interruptions from members of staff?

I was attracted by the double title of this volume: Parent-Infant Psychodynamics appealing to my adult professional self, and Wild Things, Mirrors and Ghosts, holding out the additional promise of something imaginative, with its allusion to Maurice Sendak's nursery classic, Where the Wild Things Are. I was not disappointed.

This volume sets out to explore both the interpsychic and intrapsychic impact of pregnancy, birth and early parenting, and is organized in four sections, each containing papers by distinguished contributors from the fields of research psychology, psychoanalysis, paediatrics, child therapy, social work and related disciplines. Many of these authors are writing from their own recent practice and research while others, such as Winnicott and Bion, are eminent psychoanalytic ancestors. The sections follow from ‘Face to Face: Containment and Early Exchange’ through ‘Unprocessed Residues’ and ‘Representations and Reality’ to ‘Management Issues’. These are held and linked together by the editor, Joan Raphael-Leff, who wears her formidable learning and clinical experience lightly and her own paper and introductions to each section give a sense of purpose, shape and depth to this rich selection.

This book sets out to redress a balance that is long overdue: the importance of the adult-child relationship has for too long overshadowed that of the sibling relationship, and the importance this plays in our development as children, and our adult relationships as well.

The author's cry could well be, ‘Siblings of the world unite! You have nothing to lose but your chains!’ While child psychotherapists might be well acquainted with the complex area of sibling relationships, it is quite amazing that for adult psychotherapists the subject has not been dealt with conceptually or clinically in anything like the depth it deserves.

We, too, however, may unwittingly contribute to this gap in our knowledge because of our unconscious anxiety about a potential minefield of ambivalent feelings. Or, as Prophecy Coles asks, ‘Has psychoanalytic theory, in ignoring the place siblings have in the psyche, enacted the fantasy of the jealous sibling, who hopes that if he or she ignores the other siblings they will go away?’ (p. 19). Siblings, while discriminated against and marginalized in the psychoanalytic family, are unavoidably all around us! That they are rarely deemed to have the clinical or theoretical clout necessary for serious discussion and consideration may say more about our defensiveness than the possibility of a theoretical oversight.

In this context, each chapter of this short but hard-hitting book raises questions and opens subjects for debate and discussion that have never been raised in this way before, including: sibling transference and countertransference; Freud's view of siblings linked with his own personal experience; Freud's treatment of the Wolf Man case as linked with his self-analysis; how identification with siblings contributes to adult sexuality and relationships as well as the importance of sibling relationships in mental health; sibling incest - why it happens, when it is harmful, or not; brotherly and sisterly love; what makes the sibling experience different from the parent-child experience.

Editorial

Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

[BJP@jarundale.demon.co.uk]

Jean Arundale  

Considering that Freud believed free association to be the ‘fundamental rule’ of psychoanalysis, he wrote very little about how it worked in practical terms. He stated simply that the patient is to say whatever comes involuntarily into his or her mind, and to be as honest as possible, not holding anything back. Then the analyst, listening with ‘free floating attention’ to every detail, makes connections, allowing a unique sort of dialogue to be set up which is different from ordinary conversation or purposeful intellectual tasks, and in which the unconscious of the patient and the analyst come as closely together as possible in the search for pathogenic influences in the patient's life.

This is not so easy as it sounds, as we know. Freud attributes the difficulty to dynamic forces in the mind at work in active opposition to one another. In his view, unruly unconscious infantile or primitive thoughts and emotions push upward to gain ascendancy, to have their way with the individual, which are strongly opposed by the civilized adult as unacceptable. Of course, with some patients, everything is right there ‘in our face’ waiting to be understood. But for most and for much of the time, the analytic therapist must find ways to lift repressions and to loosen resistances in order to dig into deeper levels, and the main tool is free association.

This technique developed by Freud for exploring the human mind grew out of hypnosis and has been proved to be practically fruitful by generations of psychoanalysts and psychotherapists. All the talking cures today originate from this ingenious notion. All well and good, but not quite so simple. Many unanswered questions arise when one looks closely. For example, Freud didn't indicate whether the function of free association is mainly to provide a baseline to which to return when conscious work dries up or whether the fundamental rule is to be applied strictly and systematically. That is, does the analyst insist upon the patient producing free associations, dismantling purposive or evasive communications and waiting for the real thing? If so, how does the analyst most effectively do this?

Sherly Williams

Sherly Williams  

How do therapists evolve beyond formal training and qualification? What began as a personal question born out of my own distance in time from the training I undertook to become a therapist, and my subsequent involvement in the training of other therapists, suddenly acquired a topical significance when the UKCP document on ‘Continuing Professional Development’ dropped through my mailbox. A balanced and thoughtful document accentuating the centrality of reflective practice and the need for personal development, its main thrust nevertheless is towards the external world. Its methodology is chiefly bureaucratic, necessitating policies to be developed and implemented by member organizations. ‘Continuing Professional Development’ (CPD) aims to continue for practitioners the process of verification and accountability to the profession and to the general public that the qualifying process entailed. Yet we belong to a profession that has a unique distinction - we point not only to diplomas and competencies, but also to the therapist's capacity to participate in his personal development. This casts a different light altogether on how the clinician derives his authority. Jung writes of the requirement for a personal analysis in the training of analysts:

We have learned to place in the foreground the personality of the doctor himself as a curative or harmful factor; and that what is now demanded is his own transformation … as soon as psychotherapy takes the doctor himself for its subject, it transcends its medical origins and ceases to be merely a method for treating the sick. (Jung 1929, pp. 74, 75)

This will be the subject of my paper which will address the therapist's own development - a matter that inevitably goes beyond the compass of any CPD policy, and yet remains embedded in the discharge of professional responsibilities.

Fiona Gardner

Fiona Gardner

11 Chaucer Road, Bath BA2 4QU. [email: fgardner@fish.co.uk]

Fiona Gardner  

This paper explores the dynamics involved for children growing up with a narcissistic parent. It suggests that as a consequence of a malignant identification children resort to compliance and sacrifice in varying degrees. Compliance, as part of the sacrificial dynamic, also serves as a means for identification, which in the absence of other emotional nurturance the infant and later the child is reluctant to relinquish. Drawing on the personal and professional experiences of both D.W. Winnicott and H.J.S. Guntrip the paper discusses the underlying conflict between absorption into and abandonment from the narcissistic parent. The psychotherapeutic relationship offers a space to acknowledge the systematic interconnectedness that is at the heart of the malignant identification and the terrible dependency involved. Through a good personal relationship a benign identification with the therapist can begin to replace what was previously so strongly held onto. Brief extracts from two incomplete psychotherapies with young men are used to illustrate certain aspects of the therapeutic work involved.

Caroline Garland

Caroline Garland

120 Belsize Lane, London NW3 5BA. [email: Cbgarland27hh@cs.com]

Caroline Garland  

In this paper I want to describe some of the obstacles for a particular patient in the way of her being able to achieve a freedom of thought (Segal 1977) and an accompanying freedom of speech - that is to say the expression of those thoughts out loud to me. By ‘freedom of thought’ I mean something that goes deep as well as wide. It includes the emotional depth that has its origins in the unconscious, as well as the dimension of time - that is to say, the meaning and significance of historical events. In my patient there was a marked ‘horizontal’ split between the breadth of her cognitive capacities and the depths of her unconscious phantasy. And, although the facts of her own history were known to her, their significance seemed to be missing. I am going to try to show how, during the course of her analysis, she moved from a position in which her freedom of thought was limited and restricted to one in which a greater degree of mental movement was possible, in terms of these three dimensions of space, depth and time. I shall speculate on the factors that had restricted her movement in the first place, and on those subsequent experiences that seemed to be helpful in freeing it up. And I shall conclude by suggesting that ‘free association’ in a modern analysis can be taken usefully to include the way a patient links up with - associates with - his or her objects, internally and externally, by showing how my patient became more able to perceive and tolerate her objects' links with each other.

Freud's original notion of ‘free association’ really derives from a different epoch in the history of psychoanalysis, a time when he hoped it might create in waking life the conditions of dream. Freud felt it to be the path (if not quite as broad as the ‘royal road’) which could, if the analyst were a sufficiently sensitive, open-minded and keen-eared tracker, be established between that which was unconscious and irrational, and that which was conscious and rational.

Michael Richards

Michael Richards

London

Michael Richards  

The philosopher Karl Popper, working in Alfred Adler's Vienna child clinic in 1919, brought a case to Adler that he thought might refute Adler's theory (about inferiority). Adler said that he couldn't accept Popper's refutation. ‘Why?’ asked Popper. ‘Because of my hundred-fold clinical experience,’ replied Adler. To which Popper replied, ‘And I suppose next time you will refer to your hundred-and-one-fold clinical experience’.

Popper frequently came into my mind while reading this book because of his important contribution in demarcating science from other human endeavours. He (Popper 1959) pointed out that you don't prove scientific theories by finding cases to support them; instead you refute (or modify) them by finding cases that are inconsistent with their predictions. This important book takes up Popper's implicit challenge to psychoanalysis to demonstrate that it belongs on the scientific side of his demarcation. It is also worth recalling that, unlike the positivist philosophers, Popper did not regard human endeavours on the non-scientific side as worthless. They were valuable in helping us make sense of our human journey but could not be demonstrated to be objectively true, i.e. they were not open to falsification. Marxism, religion and psychoanalysis were judged non-scientific in this sense and he used to elaborate this by claiming that no imaginable event would stop followers of one these disciplines from continuing their allegiance. I will return to this issue.

Peter Fonagy and Mary Target have made it their aim both to describe and to evaluate all the major psychoanalytic theories in use in the English-speaking world, Lacanian theory excepted. The book seemed during my reading to call for two reviews: one to comment on the choice and treatment of the theories described, and one to comment on the authors' critique of these theories and on psychoanalysis in general. But this thought merely reminds one how unusual is their approach. I don't recall during my training much discussion of the evidence adduced in support of Klein's or Kohut's ideas; the fact that they had followers made them worth studying. And presumably the fact that they had followers meant that their ideas were found to be valuable in the consulting room.

Ann Scott  

From the Editor:

In this issue the BJP publishes two letters about The College of Psychoanalysts - United Kingdom. One is from its President, Jacques China. One is from a critic of The College, Carola Thorpe. Opinion within the Editorial Board about publishing them has been strongly divided. The final decision has been mine as Editor, and in reaching my decision to publish, I have taken my colleagues' views carefully into account. I want to register them here.

My personal view about the letters derives at source from my commitment to ‘engagement with difference’, a phrase I used in my Editorial in BJP 19(4). The BJP is in a good position, in my view, to make an ongoing space for debate about professional and organizational dynamics and developments, be this about neutral or more sensitive matters. Both letters set out important terms of debate, and in my view the claims for publication outweigh the arguments against.

In favour of publication, in addition, has been the free speech argument in principle, along with the general point that publication of a letter does not imply editorial endorsement. It has also been argued that the BJP does owe it to its readers to air the discussion about The College in a way that allows individual psychoanalytic psychotherapists, whatever the slant of their training organizations, to come to a considered, well-informed view about whether The College is divisive, or is making a sincere attempt to achieve pluralism in a divided profession. The correspondence is a start; further commentaries could follow, unsolicited or commissioned.

Dear Editor

We would like to draw our existence to the attention of those of your readers who may not yet have heard about us and to update all readers on some recent developments.

The College was formed with, inter alia, the following objectives:

To promote the discipline of psychoanalysis in a comprehensive, pluralistic and non-partisan manner which would recognize both non-IPA and IPA-affiliated psychoanalysts in this country, in order better to reflect the situation in the world-wide community where:

the artificial distinction between psychoanalysts and psychoanalytic psychotherapists (as opposed to the narrow but valid distinction between psychoanalysis and psychoanalytic psychotherapy) is unknown, and

psychoanalysts who have undergone a non-IPA training far outnumber those who have undergone an IPA-affiliated training.

To provide a forum for discussion, as well as for understanding and a degree of reconciliation, among psychoanalytic practitioners of all persuasions.

To provide, for the benefit of the public, a national register of psychoanalytic practitioners who have undergone a psychoanalytic training, as recognized by The College.

Initially, a very high proportion of applicants (at one time as high as 25%) was from BCP. However, following threats of loss of membership by BCP most of their registrants, though by no means all, withdrew from membership of The College. The Register of Practitioners, currently comprising 134 members, has now been published on the College website.

Carola Thorpe  

Dear Editor

I write as a registrant of both the UKCP and BCP, because I am saddened and disturbed by recent developments within our profession, namely the founding of The College of Psychoanalysts - United Kingdom. I would like to express my concerns and discover whether these are shared by BJP readers.

Along with other UKCP and BCP registrants, I received a letter inviting me to part with £25 and apply for membership of the newly created ‘College of Psychoanalysts United Kingdom’ (logo CP-UK), which would entitle me to call myself a ‘psychoanalyst’. As the note on the British Psychoanalytic Society's web page points out, the new College's web domain (www.psychoanalysts.org.uk) is remarkably similar to their own (www.psychoanalysis.org.uk); and the CP-UK, using the same initials as UKCP, seems to invite the public's confusion. I understand that the UKCP itself is registering an objection to this.

I think it can be no coincidence that this College has emerged after the decision of the UKCP in June that it would not permit the label ‘UKCP-registered psychoanalyst’ to be used. The application to register psychoanalysts was made on the basis that ‘psychoanalyst’ and ‘psychoanalytic psychotherapist’ were interchangeable, and this was rejected. The decision was reached after a process of deliberations spanning several years; a decision that some, it seems, are now unwilling to abide by. Self-regulation, as attempted by our profession, is only possible if the membership respects decisions that have been reached democratically.

Listening to Silence

First published in BJP 7(4), 1991

Andrea Sabbadini

Andrea Sabbadini

38 Berkeley Road, London N8 8RU. [email: a.sabbadini@macunlimited.net]

Andrea Sabbadini  

I have examined the function of silence - its possible role and meanings - in the psychoanalytic encounter. I have argued that silence is complementary to words in general, and to analytic free associations in particular, and that silence in the patient is often more than just the expression of his resistance. It could be useful to consider the silent space within a session as a sort of container of words - words that for complex, overdetermined, unconscious reasons cannot be uttered. I have insisted on the significance of analytic silences and warned against responding to them either through a retaliatory silence or through a flood of premature interpretations. These inadequate reactions often stem from the analyst's own anxiety evoked in him by the patient's silence. Anxiety and silence are closely connected. Each silence is a compromise formation, concealing the unconscious fantasy from which it originates, while expressing a conscious one, often related to the transference situation. It is the task of the analyst to listen to his patient's silences in order to help him understand their meanings.

The internal object concept as developed by Melanie Klein and subsequent Kleinians has increased in importance in the past 60 years. The internal world and internal space, the stratified levels of activity of part and whole objects within the internal space, their incorporation, interiorization, introjection, assimilation and non-assimilation, their projection and projective identification, their fate in the external world space and many other aspects have now become everyday problems of psychoanalysis. The subject is admirably discussed in the Dictionary of Kleinian Thought by R.D. Hinshelwood (1991).

One of the thoughts that fascinated Dr Rey was the concreteness of internal objects and their life in a person's internal space alongside their life when existing in projected form in an external object's internal space. During the treatment of psychotic and borderline child and adult patients this became even more evident. First published in BJP 11(2), 1994

J.H. Rey

J.H. Rey

J.H. Rey  

The concept of the internal objects and internal and external spaces has been further developed in this paper. These objects are an important part of patients seeking treatment for themselves for they are also looking unconsciously for ‘treatment’ of these objects. The objects are ‘damaged’ and the patient does not know how to repair them. He keeps them alive in the hope that help will come. The methods used to keep them alive, even when dying, have been described. The stages at which these objects have been, or are thought to have been, damaged is vital. For example, they can range from the sensorimotor level to higher levels of maturation, to produce psychosis, borderline or hypochondria. The concrete level is stressed for it leads to concrete repair as opposed to psychic reparation.

The So-Called ‘Death Drive’: A Sexual Drive1

Jean Laplanche

Jean Laplanche

Jean Laplanche  

This article will develop three successive perspectives:

A historical or historico-critical perspective; that is, my interpretation of the appearance of the death drive and its function in the development of Freudian thought.

A metapsychological perspective. What position are we to assign, in a metapsychology of the human being and the unconscious, to those forces which Freud described in an inappropriate manner as ‘death’ and ‘life’ drives?

A third section will concern some remarks on a question of general psychology: by what factors are we to explain the crucial affective phenomena of love and hate, without a strict adherence to Freud's conception of them?

Since 1967 I have been able, at numerous moments, to develop these ideas. I will mention three books of mine which have been translated into English: The Language of Psychoanalysis (1967), Life and Death in Psychoanalysis (1970), New Foundations for Psychoanalysis (1987).

For those readers who have little knowledge of my ideas, I will clarify my position in advance with some general statements. These proposals are expressed here in a somewhat radical form.

The supposed originary conflict between life and death drives is absolutely not a biological opposition which exists in the living being, and consequently it has no pertinence to the science of biology.

This opposition is uniquely and wholly located in the domain of the human being - and not as a difference between sexuality and a non-sexual aggressivity, but in the heart of sexuality itself. If the Freudian terminology is to be retained, one should insert the adjective ‘sexual’, talking of the sexual death drives versus the sexual life drives.

Professor Laplanche's conference paper was based on ‘The so-called “death drive”: a sexual drive’, originally published in The Death Drive: New Life for a Dead Subject? edited by Rob Weatherill (Karnac, London, 1999, www.karnacbooks.com). It is reproduced by kind permission of Karnac Books and Rob Weatherill. The Journal is also grateful to John Fletcher, who has significantly contributed to the shape of ‘On Sexuality and the Death Drive’. - Ed.

Little Hope, New Hampshire. Pretty, angel-faced Suzanne Stone wants only one thing and that's to be in TV, because ‘unless you're on TV you're no-one in America’. She marries a man who will do anything to please her, indeed who with self-prophetic irony announces with the gift of lap-dog Walter that he will ‘die for her love’. Using her honeymoon to get access to a conference of the major TV networks, Suzanne then dons a designer suit, an attaché case and a French twist hairstyle as props to convince slow-moving, local cable-TV chief Ed Grant to give her a job at the station. In no time she has persuaded him to let her do the weather reports and, keen to get more projects off the ground, she starts visiting a local school to make a documentary on the aspirations of the local youth. There she meets poor, white, disaffected no-hopers, Jamie, Lydia and Russell.

Meanwhile husband Larry Marretto, whose Italian parents run a successful restaurant, is becoming dangerously keen on the idea of children and ‘family life’. Career-obsessed Suzanne, perceiving the threat to her professional future, sees an opportunity to get rid of him that will leave her career path unthreatened. She seduces Jamie, dropping into the conversation that her husband beats her, draws Lydia into her confidence and elicits the information that Russell has a gun. Before long, Jamie has agreed to murder her husband and Suzanne has made sure that she has the perfect alibi, presenting the weather live on TV as the crime takes place.
