Assessing and Formulating Attachment Issues and Styles in Psychotherapy

Gillian Hardy , Jan Aldridge , Colin Davidson , Celly Rowe and Stephen Reilly

Stephen Reilly

Leeds LS2 9JT. [email: gillianh@psychology.leeds.ac.uk]

Stephen Reilly  

There are few attachment-based measures designed for use by therapists to inform the clinical process of psychotherapy. The aim was to develop an attachment based interview schedule for use by mental health professionals. A draft interview schedule was developed through a review of the literature. Systematic analysis of case materials led to refinements of the schedule. Attachment formulations were developed for six patients. The clinical validity of these formulations was assessed through group discussion and via reports from the patients' therapists. The schedule provided information about patients' attachment histories, styles, issues and problems leading to an attachment formulation, possible foci for therapeutic work, and difficulties that might arise during therapy. The interview schedule allows a picture to be built up of how attachment patterns and behaviours have developed and how they are expressed in the present. It leads to hypotheses about what needs to change for the individual to have more secure, less distorted relationships and what problems may be encountered during therapy.

Diana Birkett

Diana Birkett

Centre for Psychoanalytical Psychotherapy, London

Diana Birkett  

This book is not an easy read; but then, why should it be? If the word ‘counter-intuitive’, when applied to the subject of sado-masochism did not beg so many questions, it might well seem appropriate to describe an area which the author therefore goes to great pains to identify, differentiate and come to some very definite conclusions about. The book boasts two forewords, the first by Eric Brenman, who quotes from the text to define the

341

author's intention: ‘Metaphysically speaking my aim is the isolation within a complex organism of a cell that I call the sado-masochistic monad in which I place the mental experience of destructive pleasure’ (p. 4).

Before attempting to reach this aim, De Masi makes the startling and rather convincing claim that, in spite of the huge importance accorded to sexuality in psychoanalytic theory, ‘psychoanalysts, like researchers in other disciplines, find themselves unable to penetrate in depth its intimate essence’ (p. 2). He therefore chooses to start from a phenomenological rather than a theoretical approach, in an attempt to understand ‘the central importance of sexual pleasure and the power it exerts over the psychic life of the individual’ (p. 3). From these excerpts it may be apparent that De Masi regards sexuality, and perversion in particular, as a predominantly mental phenomenon. After taking us through some historical material, such as Krafft-Ebing's observations, some ideas on ascetic masochism, and reviewing the case of the Wolf Man, he begins to wrestle with problems of definition. This is the most difficult part of the book to read, as he is clearly disagreeing with much of existing theory without first having described it, and it is not until Chapter Eight that the dominant theories are outlined in sufficient detail for his deviation from them to be really clear (I would suggest that any reader not steeped in sado-masochistic theory begin with this chapter).

Here are summarized the three paradigms which, although ‘distinguishing themselves from one another, stand in a relationship of contiguity, pursuing different routes towards understanding the reality they seek to investigate’ (p. 45). The first, which he calls the Freudian psychosexual, sees perversion along a continuum from infant sexuality, although only one or two aspects of polymorphism are reproduced in adult behaviour. This behaviour is seen as a defence against castration anxiety, and involves a regression of the libido as a way of circumventing the resolution of the Oedipus complex. Later ideas about the death-drive, and the theory of fusion of drives, are invoked to elaborate on masochism as something more than an inversion of sadism. Chasseguet-Smirgel is considered the chief modern exponent of the paradigm, though De Masi considers the Freudian approach an over-simplification because of its insistence on drive theory. The second paradigm, derived from the ideas of Winnicott and Kohut, is the relational one, in which perversion is seen as essentially defensive: if the complex process of interaction between the infant and his environment goes wrong, then sexual development may also take an anomalous form, and the child may attempt to sustain his damaged sense of self through masturbatory activities. This sexualization is distinguished from drive theory by being defined as a secondary phenomenon: ‘the drive appears as a disintegration product … enacted in the fantasies and actions of the pervert’ (Kohut 1997). One of the functions of the sexual activity is in the structuring of the self, and as a defence against relational anxieties.

Drawing on ideas from the psychoanalytic thought of Bion and the philosophy of Whitehead the paper explores the difference between ‘prehended lust’ and perverse sexuality. Prehended lust is regarded as life-enhancing whereas in perverse sexuality excitement is generated to disencumber the individual of anxiety. This view is illustrated by clinical material and by a more lengthy discussion of the recent British film The Principles of Lust, directed by Penny Woolcock.

Pseudo-Free Association: The Sophisticated Analytic Patient and ‘As-If’ Relating

Chris Mawson

Chris Mawson

112a Shirland Road, London W9 2EQ. [email: editors@psychoanalysis.org.uk]

Chris Mawson  

Introduction

When is a free association not a free association? You will notice that I have couched this question in the same format as an old riddle or joke but, unlike that structure, it has no quick and clever answer. Instead I will try to open up the question and make it relevant to the themes emerging in this conference - free association and the workings of the unconscious mind. Although I have spoken of a free association, this is a short-hand term. I doubt that it makes sense to think of a free association as a unit in isolation from its immediate context. If the field created between patient and analyst is not free-associative in its basic processes, then the elements being produced may resemble free associations in appearance only.

The main argument in this paper is that the connection between ‘as-if’ relating and pseudo-free association is the importance to the patient of what Bion called the uninterrupted validation of their daydreamed self. I hope I may be able to make this clearer as I go on.

Long before I was invited to talk at this conference, the question forming the subtitle of my talk today came to me as I listened to a patient, Mr R, a 35-year-old man who had been in analysis with me for four years, a man who just could not free associate. He would, however, talk as though he could. He told me regularly and earnestly that what he was about to say had just come into his mind. He would say, with a cheery, lilting tone, ‘I can't imagine why I am thinking of this but …’; ‘Heaven knows why this has just popped into my mind …’, and I would notice that I had begun to feel somewhat enlivened and even a little hopeful of meaningful communication; now I would be able to do some work - only to discover a little later that both of us had been speaking empty words with great confidence.

CHRIS MAWSON is a psychoanalyst. A Member of the British Psychoanalytical Society, he first trained as a clinical psychologist and worked initially with adolescents and children, beginning at the Tavistock Clinic. He now works in private practice, and is interested also in the study of groups and organisations from a psychoanalytic perspective, particularly that pursued by the British group relations orientation. Jean Arundale

Jean Arundale

11 Albert Place, London W8 5PD. [email: ja@jarundale.demon.co.uk]

Jean Arundale  

We take the life instincts somewhat for granted in our psychoanalytic theory and practice, the drive to experience, to love, to learn and to grow - the instinctual life force that Freud termed the libido, which he went on to elaborate in regard to the different forms libido takes from infancy through the various stages to adulthood. That there are obstructions and impediments to the life force in individuals is also assumed, but how we think about these anti-developmental forces is arguable. Attempts to conceptualize these occur throughout Freud's writing (fixations, defences, resistances, repetitions and so on) and in the writing of many others. However, Freud's most striking idea is of a primal death instinct, an anti-life force in place at the very beginning of infant life that strives to foreclose the terrors involved in survival and being alive by establishing a state of quiescence or death. Based on the biological principles of his day, he believed the helpless infant is overwhelmed in the face of the inflaming, disturbing stimuli of being alive. Thus Freud put forward his most controversial and paradoxical notion that death is free from tension and desire, and is thus the ultimate pleasure.

In discussing these larger issues of life and death, Freud enters the arena of philosophy. There are, however, many clinicians who employ these concepts in clinical practice, and see psychoanalysis itself becoming a struggle between these elemental forces. A number of contemporary British thinkers including Segal, Feldman, and Britton have identified the death instinct in the clinical setting as attacks on the progress of analysis, as assaults on awareness, thinking or any emotional liveliness. Elizabeth Andrew

Elizabeth Andrew

London

Elizabeth Andrew  

Gertrud Mander Writes:

We are taking the unusual step of publishing two reviews of Inconceivable Conceptions: Psychoanalytic Aspects of Infertility and Reproductive Technology edited by Jane Haynes and Juliet Miller, because of the subject's newness and importance and the interesting difference of approaches. One review was commissioned, written by the family therapist Elizabeth Andrew, the other review was sent in unsolicited, written by the analytical psychologist Nicola Glucksmann.

IN A Year When Reports about further advances in assisted reproduction and lively discussions about the clinical, psychological, social, moral and ethical implications of these developments are appearing almost daily, this is a welcome book. The editors, Jane Haynes and Juliet Miller, both psychotherapists, are clear that, while they do not dispute that the new treatments have brought many benefits and many wished-for births, there are growing concerns that ART (Assisted Reproductive Technology) has contributed to a destructive split between mind and body. Most of the contributors agree and seek to find a balance. ‘ART is neither a science of fertility, nor a science of infertility - it is about isolating, refining and juggling the mechanics of conception’ (Introduction, p. 4). The purpose of this book is to explore some of the complexities of the present situation, work towards greater understanding of the psychology of infertility and think about how a synthesis between psyche and soma might be achieved.

Since the seemingly miraculous birth by IVF of Louise Brown 25 years ago, treatment for infertility has developed so fast that it is now possible for two people, who have contributed neither egg nor sperm to the process, to produce a child who has no biological connection with them. We have entered the era of the four-parent child and mothers come in three categories. In addition to those who suffer from unexplained infertility or infertility caused by disease, each year more women and their partners seek help with conception as they leave the bearing of children too late for their natural fertility.

Michael Sinason

London

Michael Sinason  

Dear Editor

In her paper on suicide (BJP 20(3), 2004), Marguerite Valentine says that her patient experienced his parents as living in his head. He said that he ‘felt truly colonized by an occupying, alien force, over which he had little control’. Valentine quotes Searles' 1959 paper in which he says that this type of internal alienation is difficult to resolve because the therapist becomes caught up in a reconstituted patient-parent symbiotic relatedness in the transference. Searles makes the point that this is not simply a matter of countertransference but arises also because psychotherapists may choose this profession in reaction formation to their own unconscious propensity for symbiotic relating. In consequence, in the hot seat of the therapeutic encounter it is easy for patterns of interaction to occur that can only be understood in retrospect. When Valentine's patient expressed a desire to ‘come off’ medication it presented an opportunity for the therapist to make it a condition of further psychotherapy that the patient consent to her having direct contact with the psychiatric team. In 1976 Searles wrote: ‘I had to develop respect for the limit-setting function as being an inherent part of the analyst's work and, in fact, fundamental to all his “higher” analytic functions.’ He argues that this is needed because the therapist can otherwise become ‘isolated and threatened, singled out from colleagues, in relation to whom, the patient contrasts the therapist negatively’.

It may have been because the patient felt increasingly paranoid about the claustrophobic symbiotic transference relationship that he took up the offer of an appointment for NHS psychotherapy assessment. Eventually, he shouted at the therapist that she should not talk or listen to him and should contact the doctor who would tell her to stop the sessions.

Cross-Gender Identifications in Heterosexual Couples

First published in BJP 11(4), 1995

A well-established sense of gender does not depend on sexual object choice but on a sense of security in belonging to the gender correlated to one's biological sex. Cross-gender identifications are often found in heterosexual couples who show a marked reversal of conventional gender norms and whose typical interaction constitutes a shared defence against their mutual lack of gender security. Both partners are ‘possessed’ by the contrasexual archetype (anima and animus) and have been unable to integrate their contrasexual potential. Three aetiological factors seem to predispose both men and women towards cross-gender identification: an over-close relationship with the parent of the opposite sex, a negative identification with the parent of the same sex, and inappropriate use by their mothers as substitute caretakers (‘narcissistic objects’). In both sexes masculinity is idealized while femininity is denigrated.

Othello: Faith and Doubt in the Good Object Introduction

Bernardine Bishop

Bernardine Bishop

7 Patshull Road, London NW5 2JX. [email: bernardinebishop@yahoo.co.uk]

Bernardine Bishop  

I wrote this paper, I now see, nearly 10 years ago. It started life as a very personal series of thoughts and connections arising directly from the hot heart of experience in my own analysis. And it still seems, reading it now nearly 10 years later, to bear the marks in its writing of the intensity of immediate emotional discovery. But at the same time as being very personal, it also appears to me, from the vantage point of the present, as a very small but seaworthy boat in a big flotilla travelling along the mainstream of the development of post-Kleinian thought.

I trace one of the colours of this development mostly to Meltzer. Some would say Bion, but for me it's Meltzer. I mean the development whereby words like truth, goodness, beauty, mystery, faith, can now be used unblinkingly in the post-Kleinian consulting room, becoming part of the currency of daily analytic exchange. What has happened, I believe, is that an emphasis has shifted towards the good object and its dynamic properties within the self, and away from the many psychic forces which attack, impede and harass the introjection and subsequent stability of that object. It is a shift of emphasis only: the negative elements are not denied or trivialized. Iago remains Iago. But perhaps the play of new light has disclosed more hopeful and creative possibilities.

Something I was and remain very interested in when I wrote this paper is what happens in the personality when that which occupies the position of the good object is actually not good. This was my point about what Othello projects on to Desdemona. When Othello falls in love, Desdemona becomes for him what has the place and potency in him of the good object, but the internal object which is his to project is fickle and untrustworthy. Because of its untrustworthy nature, the carrier of the projection, poor Desdemona, can only be good so long as she is enthroned and imprisoned

Othello: Faith and Doubt in the Good Object

First published in BJP 12(3), 1996

This paper considers Shakespeare's tragedy of Othello as a symbolic enactment of intrapsychic life. The developmental movement from the paranoid-schizoid to the depressive position and from narcissistic love, arising from the investment of parts of the self in another person, to real, interpersonal love, is arrested and finally ruined by the agency of a split-off Iago element in the personality. Faith in the good object is thereby perverted into doubt. The mechanisms whereby this happens are discussed in terms of Othello's devaluation of Desdemona in the growing presence of pathological processes.

Steven Mendoza  

Here is another exemplary book from Dr Britton who describes it as ‘a personal reappraisal of psychoanalytic theories in the light of clinical experience’ (p. ix). On the next page he makes it clear that his purpose is not only that we should benefit from his experience but also from our own. He explains that in psychoanalysis, ‘The acquisition of personal experience is very slow, and therefore the reliance on the authority of others is protracted’ (p. x). His book reappraises psychoanalytic theories with scholarship as well as clinical experience and all of us will learn from both aspects. The knowledgeable and experienced will not feel that their time is being wasted; the trainee will learn not only metapsychology but its realization in the consulting room and the feel of how ideas inform and are informed by clinical work.

In Part One, ‘Sex and Death’, the death instinct is reappraised as a function not of death itself but of destructiveness directed not inward at the self but outward at the object. On page 3 he says that the ‘desire for a love-object … is primary’. Here he seems to go beyond Klein's principle of an ego from the beginning of life to the principle of primary love which pervades the British School of object relations and is expressed by Balint (1968) in The Basic Fault (p. 179). Later he refers to Fairbairn's (p. 118) concept of the antilibidinal ego in his discussion of the ego-hostile superego. More generally there is an openness of mind to a variety of schools of psychodynamic thought. Even Jung and his followers, in the discussion of Sabina Spielrein (p. 27), are accorded some place in his reappraisal. Kohut and Kernberg are discussed too. This is more consistent with the breadth and depth of Britton's recourse to literary and religious antecedents of psychoanalytic thought.

The discussion of hysteria is illuminating and the dismissal of it as a ‘larval psychotic state’ (p. 1) serves as a basis for an extended account of borderline conditions as organizations in their own right, not transitional states between neurosis and psychosis. With this goes a free account of the pitfalls of the erotic hysterical transference and the dangers of the analyst's collusion in the countertransference with consequent sexual misconduct. The peccadilloes of Masud Khan are mentioned and with them the need to understand the danger of the incidence of countertransference neurosis instead of the use of countertransference. The psychotherapeutic house is being put in order by means of a technical understanding of how these mishaps come about.

The publication by Free Association Books of these two books, on the question of time and psychoanalysis, has added to the increasing amount of Green's work which has been translated into English. His work has come to represent an entente cordiale between the Anglo-Saxon and Continental traditions. Writing in French he encourages a critical engagement with different theories and credits Lacan, Bion and Winnicott as major influences. Green notes that, while philosophy has given a lot of attention to the question of time, psychoanalysis has given some thought to space but time remains a latent albeit central theme - a situation that he attempts to rectify. In Time in Psychoanalysis: Some Contradictory Aspects (2002) his exegesis highlights the implications of the timelessness of the unconscious, the imperative of repetition, infantile amnesia, Nachträglichkeit, primal fantasies and the question of historical truth. Diachrony in Psychoanalysis (2003) is a collection of his papers on these same themes spanning the years between 1967 and 1994 and can be read as tracing the development of his thought in Time in Psychoanalysis: Some Contradictory Aspects. In both books Green sets out to explore the relation of time to the unconscious and to examine what the psychoanalytic hypothesis of the unconscious tells us about time.

Green initially trained as a psychiatrist before qualifying as a psychoanalyst. In the early 1960s he attended Lacan's seminar for six years whilst also frequently visiting London where he became familiar with the work of Bion and Winnicott. In 1975 at a conference in London with Anna Freud presiding he presented a ground-breaking paper entitled ‘The analyst, symbolization and absence in the analytic setting’ in which he warned of a crisis in psychoanalysis. He spoke of the need to respond to patients who were suffering from a borderline condition which he characterized by the stopping of time, the failure of symbolization and the decathexis of the object. He went on to develop these concerns in his extended paper ‘The dead mother’ (1986) which won him many readers in English-speaking countries. It spoke to the challenges that many clinicians were facing and, to mark the effect of this paper on theory and technique, Routledge (London) in 1999 published a festschrift in honour of his contribution, entitled The Dead Mother (ed. Gregorio Kohon).

Do not be deceived: this fine book is about far more than Jungian psychology. Knox, a psychiatrist and Jungian analyst, has taken as her thesis an integration of leading results from psychology and neuroscience to prune and vitalize not only aspects of Jungian theory, particularly the archetype, but also key concepts in psychoanalysis as a whole - the role of the death instinct, the origin of internal objects, the origin of unconscious phantasy. In addition, and more importantly, her project serves as a model for what we all should be doing in the interests of the development of psychoanalysis as a discipline: pruning, revising, and revitalizing the theoretical frameworks of our respective theoretical orientations in the interest of further healthy growth.

Knox's thesis, supervised by Peter Fonagy and John Morton, two of our strongest stalwarts, long experienced at fighting their corners in psychoanalysis and psychology respectively for forward-looking, inclusive and accurate understandings of human psychology, is a careful, considered journey through the relevant literature in the interests of contributing to our understanding of how human subjectivity (the emergent mind) is formed developmentally.

As her book makes clear, the evidence is now overwhelming that the human infant is not born with encoded meanings of experience. Among other things, there is no room on a genome of only 30,000 genes for innate ideas or any structure such as an archetype that has the capacity to give prior meaning to experience. Such structures are learned, that is to say, are acquired developmentally, rather than inherited genetically. Thus neonatal research shows that the human infant probably has an inherited capacity to orient towards the human face. But the infant must learn the meaning and significance to it of the mothering person's face. Mother as archetype is (a) not inherited genetically, nor (b) are there inherited brain structures that order the infant's experience into a universal archetype, nor is the archetypal Mother (c) a transcendent reality, a metaphysical (Platonic) thing that exists fully formed in a transcendent space independently of culture, history and biology.
